messages.content: I want to design a persistent-memory transactional index that combines serializable concurrency, crash-safe memory reclamation, and recovery independent of total index size. It must recover after every injected persistence-boundary crash without losing acknowledged commits or resurrecting reclaimed records. Recovery must read at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of the number of completed transactions. How should I frame the design?

Frame it as three obligations that must hold together, not as separate features. Concurrent transactions must have serializable outcomes; an acknowledgment must survive any subsequently injected persistence-boundary crash; and reclamation must remain safe across that crash, so recovery cannot bring a reclaimed record back as live. The recovery procedure must establish those facts while staying within the read budget of 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, regardless of how many transactions have completed.
What does it mean for those obligations to hold together?

A transaction can appear serializable during normal execution yet still fail the overall goal if its acknowledged result disappears after a crash. Similarly, reclamation can appear safe before a crash yet fail if recovery interprets persistent state in a way that revives a reclaimed record. The design has to give a consistent account of transaction outcomes and record lifetimes both before and after recovery, within the stated read limit.
Is serializability the same as preserving acknowledgment order?

Not by itself. Serializability asks whether concurrent transactions have an outcome equivalent to some serial execution. The separate durability requirement says that once a commit has been acknowledged, recovery must not lose it. The goal states both requirements; it does not specify a stronger ordering rule merely by using the word “serializable.”
So could I treat acknowledgment as a distinct boundary in the design?

Yes, as a point the design must define precisely. For every commit it acknowledges, the persistent state available after any injected persistence-boundary crash must suffice to preserve that commit. That is an obligation, not a choice of a particular persistence or acknowledgment mechanism.
And what exactly has to be true of reclaimed records after recovery?

A record that has been reclaimed must not reappear as a live record because recovery consults stale or incomplete persistent state. This is distinct from preserving acknowledged commits: a recovered index could retain commits and still be wrong if it resurrected something already reclaimed. The design needs to make both properties hold at every specified crash boundary.
Does the requirement say how reclamation has to work?

No particular reclamation mechanism is specified. The requirement is about its observable safety across persistence-boundary crashes. Whatever mechanism the design chooses must leave recovery able to distinguish records that remain valid from records that must not be revived, without exceeding the recovery-read budget.
How should I interpret “after every injected persistence-boundary crash”?

Treat it as a universal condition over the injected crash points: at each persistence boundary where a crash is injected, restarting from the resulting persistent state must preserve acknowledged commits and must not resurrect reclaimed records. Passing only a convenient subset of those points would not satisfy the stated condition. The requirement does not, on its own, prescribe a particular crash-injection procedure.
What makes the recovery-read condition different from just asking for fast recovery?

It puts an explicit limit on data read during recovery: at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index. A claim that recovery is merely “fast” would not establish that bound. Nor does the read limit alone establish a bound on every other aspect of recovery, such as computation or elapsed time.
Is the 64 MiB figure a fixed limit even if the index is larger than 100 GiB?

The stated limit is 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index. It is expressed relative to index size, rather than as a single 64 MiB ceiling for every possible index size. At the same time, recovery is meant to be independent of the *total* index size in the sense that it must not need to read the entire index to recover.
I also said recovery must be independent of the number of completed transactions. Why state that separately?

Because an index could avoid a full-index scan yet still make recovery read an ever-growing amount of transaction history. At a given index size, completing more transactions must not by itself force recovery past the 64 MiB-per-100 GiB read budget. The read requirement constrains both dependence on index contents and dependence on accumulated transaction count.
Does that rule out retaining any transaction history?

It does not rule out retaining history as such. It rules out a recovery procedure whose required reads grow with completed transaction count beyond the stated budget. The design would need to explain how recovery obtains what it needs without assuming it can read an unbounded record of completed transactions.
Can we describe a design at a high level without choosing an index structure or a reclamation algorithm yet?

Yes. At the specification level, describe how a concurrent transaction acquires a serializable outcome, what persistent evidence makes an acknowledged commit recoverable, what prevents reclaimed records from being treated as live on restart, and how recovery finds enough evidence within its read budget. Those are interfaces between the obligations, not commitments to a particular index layout, concurrency-control method, or allocator.
What would be the key question at the interface between commits and reclamation?

Whether a post-crash interpretation can preserve every acknowledged commit while also respecting every reclamation that must remain effective. The design cannot establish commit durability using one interpretation of persistent state and reclamation safety using an incompatible one. Both claims have to hold for the same recovered state at each injected persistence-boundary crash.
Could a recovery procedure satisfy the read limit but still fail the goal?

Certainly. Reading little data is not sufficient if that data cannot reliably establish the required recovered state. A procedure that stays under 64 MiB per 100 GiB but loses an acknowledged commit, resurrects a reclaimed record, or yields outcomes inconsistent with serializable transactions would still fail the combined goal.
Could the reverse also happen: correct recovery that reads too much?

Yes. Preserving acknowledged commits and not resurrecting reclaimed records would meet the crash-safety requirements, but it would not excuse recovery reads above 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index. The read bound is an independent acceptance condition, including when many transactions have completed.
How would you state the complete target in one compact paragraph?

Design a persistent-memory transactional index whose concurrent transaction outcomes are serializable. After every injected persistence-boundary crash, recovery must retain all acknowledged commits and must not resurrect reclaimed records. To do so, recovery must read no more than 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, with the amount it needs to read remaining independent of the number of completed transactions.

For the persistent-memory transactional index, I propose serializable optimistic validation, copy-on-write roots, dual 8 MiB commit manifests, and lazily loaded generation-tagged free maps. How do these pieces fit the goal?

They divide the work into related concerns. Serializable optimistic validation addresses the outcome of concurrent transactions. Copy-on-write roots offer a way to represent a prospective index state without treating an in-place, partially completed change as the committed state. The dual 8 MiB commit manifests are proposed as bounded places to find commit information during recovery. Lazily loaded generation-tagged free maps address how reclamation state can be represented without requiring recovery to read every free map. The proposal still needs a precise account of how these pieces jointly preserve acknowledged commits and prevent reclaimed records from reappearing after every injected persistence-boundary crash.
What does “serializable optimistic validation” commit us to, without choosing a particular validation algorithm?

It commits the design to checking a transaction’s tentative work against relevant concurrent activity before accepting it as committed, so the accepted outcomes are equivalent to some serial execution. “Optimistic” describes the approach of proceeding tentatively and validating rather than assuming every tentative transaction can commit. The proposal does not specify the validation rules or the transaction representation; those would need to be detailed before serializability could be established.
Does serializable validation also make a commit crash-safe?

No. Validation addresses whether a commit is consistent with the other transactions. Crash safety separately requires that an acknowledged commit remain recoverable after any injected persistence-boundary crash. The design must connect the validated outcome to persistent commit evidence before it can justify acknowledgment; the proposal names components for that purpose but does not yet define the complete protocol.
Why use copy-on-write roots in this proposal?

At a conceptual level, copy-on-write roots let the design distinguish an existing committed view from a proposed updated view. That distinction is useful when a crash might interrupt an update: recovery needs a basis for selecting a valid committed view rather than treating an incomplete update as committed. Copy-on-write alone does not say which root recovery selects or when a transaction may be acknowledged.
Is a copy-on-write root the same thing as a commit record?

Not necessarily. A root can identify an index view, while commit information can establish which view is entitled to count as committed after a crash. The proposal includes both copy-on-write roots and commit manifests, but it does not specify their exact contents or how they refer to one another. That relationship is one of the important details to define.
What should I infer from “dual 8 MiB commit manifests”?

It specifies two commit manifests, each 8 MiB. Their proposed role is to make the information needed to identify committed state available through bounded recovery reads, rather than requiring a scan of the entire index or a history that grows with completed transaction count. Having two manifests does not, by itself, establish how either is updated, how recovery judges them, or whether the required read bound is met.
The two manifests are 16 MiB in total, right?

Yes: two at 8 MiB each have a combined size of 16 MiB. That arithmetic is not a measurement of recovery reads. The design must account for everything recovery actually has to read, including any information beyond the manifests, against the limit of 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index.
Could I just say recovery reads the manifests and therefore meets the limit?

Only if the complete recovery procedure really can meet its correctness obligations using reads within the limit. Naming bounded manifests does not establish that the committed root can be identified, that acknowledged commits are retained, or that reclaimed records cannot be resurrected. If recovery needs other data to establish those facts, its reads count too.
What is the point of generation tags on the free maps?

They are proposed to help distinguish reclamation state across different lifetimes of a location or record. Conceptually, a generation tag can prevent an old reference from being mistaken for a reference to a current object, provided the design checks and persists the relevant state correctly. The proposal does not yet specify the tag rules or prove that they prevent resurrection at every crash boundary.
And what does “lazily loaded” mean for recovery?

It means the design proposes not loading all free maps as a routine part of recovery, instead accessing them when needed. That supports the aim of avoiding recovery reads proportional to the whole index. Laziness cannot come at the expense of correctness, though: any decision made before a free map is loaded must still be safe, and later loading must not turn a reclaimed record into a live one.
Would deferring free-map reads simply move the recovery work somewhere else?

It can defer work, but deferral alone is not a correctness argument or a complete account of the recovery bound. The relevant question is what must be read to finish recovery and safely resume using the index. If information is essential for that, calling it lazy does not make its cost or its effect on correctness disappear. The proposal needs a clear boundary between what recovery establishes and what can safely be loaded later.
How do the manifests and free maps relate to the no-resurrection requirement?

They must support a compatible interpretation of persistent state. Commit information cannot cause recovery to accept a root that treats a reclaimed record as live, and deferred free-map loading cannot later expose such a record as live either. The proposal suggests separate places for commit and reclamation information; it still has to show how they agree after each injected persistence-boundary crash.
Could the two manifests make crash recovery safe on their own?

Their being dual and 8 MiB each does not make them crash-safe on its own. The design must say what persistent evidence each manifest represents and how recovery behaves if a crash occurs at any persistence boundary involved in changing that evidence. It also must relate that evidence to the selected copy-on-write root and to reclamation state.
Should I treat an unacknowledged transaction differently from an acknowledged one when describing the crash requirement?

The explicit durability requirement concerns acknowledged commits: none may be lost after an injected persistence-boundary crash. The proposal therefore needs a well-defined relationship between acknowledgment and recoverable commit evidence. It also needs to avoid mistaking incomplete work for an acknowledged commit, but the node does not prescribe a specific policy for every unacknowledged transaction outcome.
Where is the main concurrency-to-persistence boundary in this proposal?

It is the point where a transaction that has passed serializable validation becomes a commit that may be acknowledged and later recovered. The precise sequence has not been given. Whatever it is, a crash at any injected persistence boundary must leave recovery able to honor acknowledgments without selecting an invalid index view or reviving reclaimed records.
Does the number of completed transactions affect how I judge the manifests?

The recovery requirement says required reads must remain independent of the number of completed transactions. Thus the manifests cannot merely be a starting point for reading an ever-growing history of completed transactions during recovery. The proposal does not yet say how bounded manifests continue to provide sufficient information as transactions accumulate; that is a property the design must demonstrate.
Could the index still be large while the recovery reads remain small?

That is the intended combination. The index may have a total size much larger than the amount recovery reads, but recovery must still reconstruct a correct usable state. The numerical constraint is at most 64 MiB read per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count—not a license to scan the full index when it is large.
What should a crash analysis cover for these four components?

For each injected persistence-boundary crash, it should examine the validated transaction outcome, the root or roots visible afterward, the commit information available in the dual 8 MiB manifests, and the reclamation information represented by the generation-tagged free maps. It should then ask whether recovery preserves every acknowledged commit, avoids resurrecting reclaimed records, and stays within the recovery-read bound. That describes what must be shown; it does not assume a particular update sequence.
Is it fair to present this as an architecture rather than as a proven solution?

Yes. You can state the proposed combination—serializable optimistic validation, copy-on-write roots, dual 8 MiB commit manifests, and lazily loaded generation-tagged free maps—and explain the intended role of each. Keep the proof obligations separate from the proposal: serializable outcomes, correct recovery after every injected persistence-boundary crash, preservation of acknowledged commits, no resurrection of reclaimed records, and reads of at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index independent of completed transaction count.
How can manifest publication atomically link committed roots to free-map generations across crashes without scanning historical transactions?

At the conceptual level, make a *published manifest state* identify both the committed root and the free-map generation information needed to interpret that root. Recovery should accept that combination as one coherent state, not choose a root from one candidate and reclamation information from another. Publication then has to be a crash-safe transition between coherent states: a crash at any injected persistence boundary must leave recovery able to identify a valid combination without reconstructing it from historical transactions. The proposal names dual 8 MiB manifests, but it does not yet specify the publication protocol that would make this true.
When you say “atomically,” are you assuming an entire 8 MiB manifest can be written atomically?

No. “Atomically” here describes what recovery is allowed to *observe*: a consistent root-and-free-map-generation combination, rather than a mixture of an old and a new one. It does not assert that an 8 MiB write is a hardware-atomic operation. The design still needs a way to distinguish a complete, durable publication from an interrupted one at every injected persistence boundary.
Can the pair just be two fields in the manifest?

Putting both fields in a manifest expresses the intended association, but it does not by itself make that association crash-safe. If a crash can leave one field reflecting a proposed state and the other reflecting a different state, recovery needs a sound basis for rejecting that mixture. It must also be clear which published combination corresponds to commits that have already been acknowledged.
So what is the key invariant to write down?

One useful invariant is: every state recovery may select identifies a committed root together with reclamation-generation information that is valid for interpreting that root. A second is: after acknowledgment, recovery must have a selectable state that preserves the acknowledged commit. These invariants connect publication to both no-lost-commit and no-resurrection requirements; neither follows merely from having two manifests.
Why can't recovery choose the newest-looking root and then load whichever free map appears current?

Because “newest-looking” is not a crash-safety rule, and independently choosing a root and a free map could combine states that were never committed together. A generation-tagged free map is meaningful only under rules that say which generation is associated with the selected root. Recovery needs to establish that association from bounded, crash-valid persistent evidence, rather than infer it from an apparent age or from scanning past transactions.
Could you illustrate the mismatch without specifying an implementation?

Imagine one coherent state described as root R₁ with generation information G₁, and a proposed successor described as R₂ with G₂. If a crash leaves portions of both visible, selecting R₂ with G₁—or R₁ with G₂—has not been justified merely because both pieces exist in persistent memory. Publication needs to let recovery select a coherent combination or reject an incomplete one. Those names are just an illustration, not prescribed fields or a proposed update sequence.
How does that prevent a reclaimed record from coming back?

It is a necessary part of the argument, not the whole argument. Recovery must interpret the selected root under the reclamation-generation state linked to it, and that interpretation must not treat a reclaimed record as live. The design still has to define what its generation tags mean and show that the persistent evidence is sufficient at every injected persistence-boundary crash. A coherent pair is not automatically a *safe* pair.
And why doesn't a safe free-map generation automatically protect acknowledged commits?

Because commit preservation is a separate obligation. A recovered root could be consistent with its free-map generation yet omit a commit that was already acknowledged. The publication and acknowledgment rules therefore have to establish not only that the root and generation information match, but that the selected state retains every acknowledged commit.
What would recovery need to know about the two manifests?

It needs a reliable rule for deciding which manifest contents, if any, constitute a complete published state and which coherent state to select when both contain candidates. That rule must remain sound if a crash interrupts publication at any injected persistence boundary. The fact that there are two 8 MiB manifests supplies bounded locations to examine; it does not, without such a rule, settle validity or selection.
Does the answer require reading historical transaction records to determine which candidate won?

The design goal says it must not depend on scanning historical transactions: recovery reads are limited to at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count. Accordingly, any information required to resolve publication must be available through bounded recovery reads. The manifest proposal aims to provide such evidence, but the contents and validation rules still need to be specified.
What if the manifest only names a root, and the root points indirectly to generation information?

The question is whether the *published state* binds the root to the correct generation information in a crash-safe, recoverable way. That binding need not necessarily be represented as two adjacent fields. An indirect reference would still have to lead recovery to the matching information within its read budget, and a crash could not be allowed to turn that reference into an ambiguous or inconsistent association.
How should I think about persistence ordering without inventing a protocol yet?

State the required relationship rather than a particular sequence of low-level operations: recovery must not accept a published reference before the persistent information needed to interpret it is safe to use. Likewise, acknowledgment must not precede the point at which an injected crash can no longer cause that acknowledged commit to disappear. The exact ordering and publication mechanism remain design details to establish.
If a crash occurs while one manifest is being changed, can recovery simply use the other?

Only if the other manifest identifies a valid coherent state *and* using it preserves every commit already acknowledged before the crash. Falling back to an older state is not automatically safe: it could discard an acknowledged commit. The design must account for crashes during publication and for the acknowledgment boundary together, rather than treating the presence of a second manifest as a complete answer.
Is there also a risk in accepting the partly changed manifest instead?

Yes. Accepting an incomplete publication could select a root whose accompanying generation information is missing or inconsistent, or count a tentative change as committed without sufficient evidence. The recovery rule must distinguish complete, valid publication from interrupted publication. It must do so at each injected persistence-boundary crash, not only when updates finish normally.
Does serializable optimistic validation affect which root is eligible for publication?

It supplies the concurrency-side condition: an accepted transaction outcome must be serializable. Publication then has to make the corresponding committed state recoverable without breaking its link to reclamation information. Validation alone cannot tell recovery which persistent root and free-map generation to use after a crash, while a crash-safe manifest alone would not establish that published transactions were serializable.
Where do the lazily loaded free maps fit if recovery does not read all of them?

The published state must give recovery enough bounded information to know how to interpret or safely defer the free maps associated with its selected root. Later loading cannot change a previously safe interpretation into one that resurrects a reclaimed record. The proposal to load maps lazily helps avoid a full-index recovery scan, but it requires a precise account of which facts must be established immediately and which can safely wait.
Could recovery defer choosing the free-map generation until that map is first loaded?

It could defer loading a map, but it cannot leave the root’s relevant reclamation interpretation unconstrained if that would permit an unsafe use of the index. The choice or binding needed for safety has to be fixed by the recovered coherent state, even if the corresponding map data is fetched later. Whether a particular design can implement that distinction is something its publication and loading rules must demonstrate.
Do generation tags solve the problem if every free map has one?

Tags are useful only if the design defines how they are assigned, checked, and bound to published roots across crashes. A tag by itself does not say which state recovery should select, whether an acknowledged commit is present, or whether a reclaimed record could be interpreted as live. The question remains about the validity of the entire published root-and-reclamation association.
How would I explain the independence from completed transaction count here?

Recovery should determine the committed root and its associated free-map generation information from bounded current publication evidence, not by replaying or searching an ever-growing set of completed transactions. Even if many transactions have completed, deciding which manifest state is valid must not require reads that grow with that count. All reads required to establish a safe recovered state still count against the 64 MiB-per-100 GiB limit.
The manifests total 16 MiB. Does that leave room for other recovery reads?

Two 8 MiB manifests total 16 MiB, but that is only their combined size, not necessarily the complete recovery-read count. The requirement remains at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index. To show the limit holds, the design must account for whatever else recovery needs to read to validate publication, select the root, and handle reclamation safely; it cannot assume those reads are free.
Can I say the manifest is a summary of completed transactions?

You can describe the intended role as bounded evidence of the committed state, as opposed to a need to scan completed transactions individually. Be careful not to imply a specified summary format or claim that it is already sufficient. The open design question is precisely how manifest publication keeps that bounded evidence coherent with both the committed root and free-map generations across crashes.
What is the most direct way to phrase that open question as a design test?

For each injected persistence-boundary crash, ask: can recovery, using no more than 64 MiB read per 100 GiB of index and without reads that grow with completed transaction count, identify a valid published root and its matching free-map generation information? Does that selection preserve every acknowledged commit and avoid resurrecting every reclaimed record, while representing serializable transaction outcomes? A publication rule is adequate only if it can answer all of those together.

I have a hypothesis for the manifest-publication question: flushing root and free-map generations before publishing a checksummed inactive manifest preserves acknowledged commits without resurrecting reclaimed records, using no more than 16 MiB of recovery reads. Does that capture the idea?

Yes, as a hypothesis. It proposes an ordering—flush the root and free-map generations first, then publish the checksummed inactive manifest—and predicts two correctness properties: acknowledged commits survive recovery, and reclaimed records do not reappear. It also predicts a recovery-read bound of ≤16 MiB. Those are claims to establish for every injected persistence-boundary crash, not results that follow from the component names alone.
What is the inactive manifest doing in that statement?

It is the manifest selected for the proposed publication while another manifest is available in the dual-manifest arrangement. The hypothesis uses publication of the checksummed inactive manifest as the step that makes a root-and-free-map-generation combination eligible to be recovered as committed. It does not yet specify the exact publication operation or the rule recovery uses to select a manifest.
Why put the root and free-map generations before the manifest in the flush order?

The intended reasoning is that a manifest should not point recovery to a combination whose required root or free-map-generation state has not been made persistent. Flushing those generations before publishing the manifest aims to make the referenced state available if publication survives a crash. The hypothesis still needs to establish what counts as complete publication and how acknowledgment relates to it.
Does the word “flushing” alone prove that the root and free-map generations are safe after a crash?

No. The claim depends on the required persistence relationship actually holding at the injected boundaries. Merely naming a flush does not show that all information recovery needs is durable before the manifest can be accepted. A precise account would have to say what must be persistent and what a crash can leave visible, without assuming the intended order automatically proves the outcome.
Why include a checksum on the inactive manifest?

The checksum is proposed as part of distinguishing acceptable manifest contents from contents affected by an interrupted publication. Its presence does not by itself make publication atomic, establish which manifest represents the acknowledged state, or guarantee that a selected root matches its free-map generations. Those relationships still require a recovery and acknowledgment argument.
So “checksummed” should not be read as “guaranteed valid”?

Right. A checksum may be one condition for accepting a candidate, but the hypothesis cannot rest on the checksum alone. Recovery must be able to select a coherent, appropriately published root-and-free-map-generation combination, and its choice must preserve all acknowledged commits without resurrecting reclaimed records.
What happens to the hypothesis if a crash occurs before the inactive manifest is published?

It must show that recovery can use a valid published state without accepting incomplete work. In particular, no commit already acknowledged before that crash may be lost. The statement of the hypothesis does not specify when acknowledgment occurs, so a crash before publication is one of the cases that makes that relationship important.
What about a crash partway through publishing it?

Recovery would need to distinguish a complete publication from an interrupted one, then select a coherent state. The checksum is relevant to that proposed distinction, but whether it is sufficient has not been established. Whichever state recovery selects must satisfy both requirements concerning acknowledged commits and reclaimed records.
And if the crash happens after publication?

The hypothesis predicts that the published manifest can identify a root and free-map-generation state whose prerequisites were flushed first. It still has to show that recovery recognizes the correct published state and that every commit acknowledged by then is represented. A crash after the intended publication step is not exempt from the every-boundary requirement.
Can recovery always fall back to the other manifest if the inactive one looks incomplete?

Not automatically. Falling back is safe only if the other manifest identifies a valid state that includes every commit already acknowledged before the crash and does not resurrect reclaimed records. The hypothesis needs to cover that case explicitly; the existence of two manifests alone cannot justify losing an acknowledged commit.
Would accepting the inactive one whenever its checksum passes solve the other side of the problem?

Not on its own. A passing checksum would have to be considered alongside the publication rule and the link between the root and free-map generations. Otherwise recovery might accept contents that do not establish a fully committed, coherent state. The hypothesis is about that whole relationship, not simply about checksum verification.
Where does acknowledgment fit into the proposed order?

The hypothesis requires an acknowledgment rule under which, once a commit is acknowledged, every subsequent injected persistence-boundary crash leaves recovery able to preserve it. That means acknowledgment cannot be justified merely by finishing serializable validation or by starting a manifest publication. The precise acknowledgment point is not specified in the hypothesis, so it remains something the argument must define.
Does serializable optimistic validation help with that durability claim?

It addresses whether the concurrent outcome is serializable, not whether an acknowledged outcome survives a crash. The hypothesis concentrates on persistence and recovery: root and free-map generations are flushed before the checksummed inactive manifest is published. The validation outcome and the published recoverable state must agree, but validation alone cannot establish the durability or no-resurrection claims.
How is no resurrection connected to the free-map generation rather than just the root?

The root identifies an index view, while the associated free-map generation information bears on how reclamation is interpreted for that view. The proposed publication must bind them coherently. If recovery chose a root while using incompatible reclamation information, it could not rely on the hypothesis to rule out a reclaimed record appearing live.
Is flushing both generations before publication sufficient to show they are bound together?

It is the ordering proposed by the hypothesis, but the binding also depends on what the published manifest identifies and on how recovery interprets that identification. Two independently persistent pieces of state are not necessarily a coherent pair. The argument has to show that any manifest recovery accepts designates matching root and free-map generations.
Could the free maps still be loaded lazily under this hypothesis?

That remains consistent with the proposal, provided the published state fixes the generation information needed to interpret a free map safely when it is loaded. Lazy loading cannot let recovery or later access treat a reclaimed record as live. The hypothesis's ≤16 MiB recovery-read claim also depends on recovery not needing additional free-map reads beyond what that bound permits.
How should I read the ≤16 MiB figure?

It is the hypothesis's bound on recovery reads, not just the size of a named component. In the proposed dual-manifest arrangement, two 8 MiB manifests total 16 MiB, but reading them would consume the entire hypothesized budget. If establishing the recovered state requires other reads, those must also fit within ≤16 MiB for the hypothesis as stated to hold.
Does ≤16 MiB replace the original recovery requirement?

No. The hypothesis proposes a particular recovery-read claim of ≤16 MiB. The design goal remains recovery reads of at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count. The relationship between those limits should be assessed for the index size in question; the ≤16 MiB hypothesis should not be described merely as a restatement of the size-relative requirement.
Why mention historical transactions in the publication question if this hypothesis focuses on two manifests?

The publication question asks recovery to identify the committed root and matching free-map generations without scanning historical transactions. The ≤16 MiB recovery-read hypothesis is meant to make that feasible through bounded current publication evidence. To establish it, recovery must not quietly rely on reading an accumulating history to resolve which manifest or generation is valid.
If many transactions complete between crashes, what must remain true?

The hypothesized recovery read count must remain ≤16 MiB regardless of how many transactions have completed. Recovery must still identify the appropriate committed root and associated free-map generations while preserving acknowledged commits and avoiding resurrection. The hypothesis does not yet explain how publication maintains sufficient bounded evidence as transactions accumulate.
Is it reasonable to separate the crash argument into cases around publication?

Yes. Crashes before publication, during publication, and after publication are natural cases to consider, with attention to every injected persistence boundary within them. For each case, the question is what state recovery can select, whether that state retains every acknowledged commit, whether it excludes reclaimed records, and how many bytes recovery must read. That case split is a way to examine the hypothesis, not a claim that it has passed.
What would a counterexample to the hypothesis look like conceptually?

Any injected persistence-boundary crash after which recovery loses an acknowledged commit or resurrects a reclaimed record would contradict its correctness claim. So would a case in which recovery needs more than 16 MiB of reads to determine a safe state. A counterexample need not challenge serializability to show that this particular publication-and-recovery hypothesis is insufficient.
Can you give me a concise version that keeps the uncertainty clear?

Hypothesis: flush the root and free-map generations before publishing a checksummed inactive manifest, so recovery can select a coherent committed state after every injected persistence-boundary crash, preserve all acknowledged commits, avoid resurrecting reclaimed records, and read ≤16 MiB without scanning historical transactions. The publication, selection, and acknowledgment rules still need to be specified and checked before those outcomes can be claimed as established.

I want to run BoundaryCrash-1 on 100 GiB images. The run will crash after each root, free-map, and manifest flush, then verify commits, reclamation, and recovery bytes. Is that the right scope for evaluating the publication hypothesis?

That is the stated scope of BoundaryCrash-1. It targets the persistence boundaries relevant to the hypothesis: root and free-map generations are flushed before publication of a checksummed inactive manifest. After each injected crash, the checks should ask whether acknowledged commits remain present, reclaimed records stay reclaimed, and recovery reads stay within the hypothesized ≤16 MiB. No outcome is established until the run is performed.
Why use 100 GiB images for this run?

The activity specifies 100 GiB images, which gives the recovery-byte check a concrete index size. At 100 GiB, the original size-relative requirement is at most 64 MiB of recovery reads. The publication hypothesis makes the separate, tighter claim of ≤16 MiB. BoundaryCrash-1 can record recovery bytes against both figures without treating either as an observed result.
What does “after each root flush” mean in the test description?

It identifies a set of injection points: after each flush of root state in the sequence being tested, inject a crash and run recovery. The test then checks the recovered state and the bytes read. The activity does not specify how many root flushes occur or their internal contents, so the description should not assume a particular count or layout.
Should the same interpretation apply to free-map and manifest flushes?

Yes. BoundaryCrash-1 calls for a crash after each free-map flush and after each manifest flush as well. Each such point is a separate opportunity to observe what recovery can safely establish from the persistent state left by that boundary. The plan names those categories; it does not report what any crash reveals.
Why check all three categories rather than only crashing after the manifest flush?

The hypothesis depends on a relationship across the root, free-map, and manifest persistence steps. A crash after a root or free-map flush may leave a different persistent state from a crash after a manifest flush. Checking each named category lets BoundaryCrash-1 examine whether recovery preserves the required commit and reclamation properties throughout those transitions, rather than only after the intended publication is complete.
If recovery finds a root after a root flush, does that mean the commit should be present?

The mere presence of root data does not establish that it represents an acknowledged commit. For the commit check, the relevant question is whether recovery retains every commit that had been acknowledged before the injected crash. BoundaryCrash-1 should not equate a flush with acknowledgment unless the design’s rules make that relationship explicit.
What exactly am I verifying when I say “commits”?

For each injected crash, verify that recovery does not lose any commit acknowledged before that crash. That is the durability condition the hypothesis claims to support. The activity does not itself define an acknowledgment protocol or report which transactions were acknowledged at any point; those distinctions must remain clear when interpreting the check.
And what does the reclamation check need to establish?

It needs to establish that recovery does not resurrect reclaimed records at each injected boundary. In this proposal, that check is especially relevant to whether the recovered root is interpreted with compatible free-map-generation information. The test should assess the recovered state, not merely whether a free-map flush occurred.
Could a run pass the commit check and fail the reclamation check?

Conceptually, yes. Recovery might preserve acknowledged commits yet treat a reclaimed record as live. BoundaryCrash-1 therefore verifies commits and reclamation separately at every specified injection point. Neither property substitutes for the other.
Could it pass both correctness checks but miss the recovery-byte target?

Yes. The activity includes recovery bytes as a separate measurement. A recovered state can preserve acknowledged commits and avoid resurrection while requiring more reads than the ≤16 MiB hypothesis allows. On a 100 GiB image, recovery reads also need to be judged against the original 64 MiB-per-100 GiB requirement; the two thresholds should not be conflated.
Should “recovery bytes” include only the manifest reads?

No. For the read claim, count what recovery actually reads to establish its state, not just a component selected in advance. If it reads information beyond the manifests, those reads matter too. BoundaryCrash-1 is meant to verify recovery bytes rather than infer them from the fact that the design has dual 8 MiB manifests.
Does a 16 MiB manifest total automatically mean the measured recovery reads are ≤16 MiB?

No. Two 8 MiB manifests have a combined size of 16 MiB, but that arithmetic does not measure the recovery procedure. The run needs to observe the bytes recovery reads after each crash. Any additional required reads would have to be included when evaluating the ≤16 MiB hypothesis.
What question is most important at a free-map flush boundary?

Whether recovery can interpret the selected committed root without treating a reclaimed record as live, even though the crash occurred at that free-map persistence boundary. It must also preserve acknowledged commits and stay within the read limit. The test is not entitled to assume that flushing a free-map generation makes its relationship to a root safe; that relationship is what the hypothesis is being evaluated on.
And at a manifest flush boundary?

Ask which root-and-free-map-generation combination recovery can legitimately select from the state left by the crash, then check the same three outcomes: acknowledged commits, reclamation safety, and recovery bytes. A manifest flush is a particularly direct test of publication, but the activity does not predetermine whether recovery will accept a particular manifest at that point.
Do I need a different success criterion for each category of crash?

The underlying criteria stay the same after every injected root, free-map, or manifest flush: no acknowledged commit lost, no reclaimed record resurrected, and recovery reads within the claimed bound. What may differ is the persistent state recovery encounters at each boundary. BoundaryCrash-1 should evaluate each state against the same obligations rather than declaring some flush categories exempt.
Does this run prove recovery is independent of completed transaction count?

A run on 100 GiB images can check the recovery bytes observed in the cases it exercises. The broader requirement says reads must remain independent of the number of completed transactions. The activity as stated does not specify variations in completed transaction count, so it should not be presented as establishing that general independence by itself.
Does it cover every possible crash for the index?

It covers the injected crashes named in the activity: after each root, free-map, and manifest flush in BoundaryCrash-1. The goal calls for correctness after every injected persistence-boundary crash. Without a specified mapping from these named flush points to all possible persistence boundaries, the run should be described by its stated coverage, not as an automatic proof about unspecified crash points.
How should I keep the hypothesis distinct from what BoundaryCrash-1 will observe?

State the prediction first: the proposed flush-before-publication ordering preserves acknowledged commits, avoids resurrection, and permits ≤16 MiB recovery reads. Then state the activity: run BoundaryCrash-1 on 100 GiB images, inject a crash after each root, free-map, and manifest flush, and verify commits, reclamation, and recovery bytes after recovery. Do not write the predicted outcomes as though the run has already produced them.
If one injected crash loses an acknowledged commit, how should I describe that observation?

It would be a failure of the commit-preservation check at that injected boundary and would contradict the publication hypothesis as stated. The observation should identify the affected boundary and the fact that the commit was acknowledged before the crash. BoundaryCrash-1 has not yet reported such an observation; this is only how that kind of result would be interpreted.
What if a reclaimed record reappears instead?

That would fail the reclamation check and contradict the hypothesis’s no-resurrection claim at that boundary, even if acknowledged commits were retained. Again, it is a possible test outcome to check for, not a reported result.
What if recovery reads 17 MiB?

A measured 17 MiB would exceed the hypothesis’s ≤16 MiB recovery-read claim. On a 100 GiB image it would still be below the original 64 MiB read ceiling, but that would not make the narrower hypothesis true. No such measurement is supplied for BoundaryCrash-1.
Can you phrase the activity itself without implying a result?

Run BoundaryCrash-1 on 100 GiB images. Inject a crash after each root, free-map, and manifest flush; after every injected crash, verify that recovery retains acknowledged commits, does not resurrect reclaimed records, and record the recovery bytes to evaluate the ≤16 MiB hypothesis and the 64 MiB-per-100 GiB requirement.

BoundaryCrash-1 produced results: across 12,480 crashes, there were zero lost acknowledged commits and zero resurrected records. Recovery read at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB. How should I report that precisely?

Report it as an observation from BoundaryCrash-1: across 12,480 injected crashes, recovery lost no acknowledged commits, resurrected no reclaimed records, and read at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index. It says specifically that no *acknowledged commits* were lost in those 12,480 crashes. It does not state an outcome for every transaction that might not have been acknowledged when a crash occurred. Keeping “acknowledged” in the report preserves the scope of the observation.
And is “zero resurrected records” the same as saying reclamation can never go wrong?

No. It reports that none of the 12,480 injected crashes produced an observed resurrection of a reclaimed record. That is a concrete reclamation result for BoundaryCrash-1, not a universal assertion about every possible execution or crash outside the run.
Should I say there were 12,480 crashes in each flush category?

No. The reported figure is 12,480 crashes in BoundaryCrash-1 as a whole. There is no category-by-category count in the result, so it would be inaccurate to assign 12,480 to root, free-map, and manifest flushes separately.
Can I at least name the boundaries BoundaryCrash-1 exercised?

Yes. BoundaryCrash-1 injected crashes after root, free-map, and manifest flushes. You can identify those as the run’s named injection points while keeping the reported 12,480 as the total and not inventing a breakdown among them.
How carefully should I word the recovery-byte result?

Say “recovery read at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB.” The phrase “at most” is an upper bound; it does not say that every recovery read exactly 16 MiB. “Per 100 GiB” is part of the reported value and should not be dropped.
Would “recovery read 16 MiB” be equivalent?

No. That wording could imply an exact measurement for each recovery or an unqualified fixed amount. The evidence states an upper bound of 16 MiB per 100 GiB. It does not provide individual read counts.
Does the read result include a measured average?
No average is reported. The available result is the maximum expressed as “at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB.” It gives no median, distribution, or count of recoveries at the bound.
Can I conclude from this that recovery time was bounded too?

Not from these figures. BoundaryCrash-1 reports recovery bytes, along with the commit and reclamation outcomes; it does not report elapsed recovery time. A bound on reads is not itself a measured time bound.
What about independence from the number of completed transactions?

The result gives a recovery-read bound for the BoundaryCrash-1 observations, but it does not report a completed-transaction-count analysis. Avoid turning the observed “at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB” into a separate claim that reads have been shown to remain independent of completed transaction count in all cases.
Does the zero-commit-loss result say anything about serializability?

It addresses crash-time preservation of acknowledged commits, not the serializability of concurrent transaction outcomes. The stated BoundaryCrash-1 result does not include a serializability observation, so that property should not be inferred from the zero-loss count.
Could I say that both correctness checks passed in all the reported crashes?

Yes, if you specify the checks: across the 12,480 crashes, there were no lost acknowledged commits and no resurrected reclaimed records. Calling them “correctness checks” is fine, but avoid implying that those two observations cover every correctness property of the index.
Does the read figure have to be tied to the same run as the two zero counts?

Yes. All three reported observations belong to BoundaryCrash-1: the 12,480-crash count, zero lost acknowledged commits and resurrected records, and recovery reads of at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB. Presenting them together makes their common scope clear.
Can I say which of the two 8 MiB manifests recovery read?

Not from this evidence. The result reports total recovery reads as an upper bound; it does not give a per-manifest read trace or identify which manifest was read in a particular recovery. The numerical resemblance between two 8 MiB manifests and 16 MiB is not a substitute for that information.
Does the result establish that every manifest publication was atomic?

It establishes the stated observations after the injected crashes. It does not, by itself, describe the internal state of every manifest publication or prove that an entire manifest was written atomically. The accurate report is about recovered commits, reclaimed records, and bytes read at the exercised crash points.
What if I want a single sentence suitable for the results section?
“In BoundaryCrash-1, 12,480 injected crashes resulted in zero lost acknowledged commits and zero resurrected reclaimed records; recovery read at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index.”
Is “resulted in” too strong if the count means these failures simply were not observed?

You can make the observational wording even clearer: “Across 12,480 injected crashes in BoundaryCrash-1, we observed no lost acknowledged commits or resurrected reclaimed records, and recovery read at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index.” That retains every reported quantity without claiming more than the run reports.
Let's adopt ordered root/free-map flushes and checksummed inactive-manifest publication. BoundaryCrash-1 verified crash safety with 16 MiB recovery reads. How should I state the decision?

State that the design will use ordered root/free-map flushes before publishing a checksummed inactive manifest. BoundaryCrash-1 verified the crash-safety properties at its injected boundaries, with recovery reading at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index. That gives the decision and its stated basis without implying that every possible crash or concurrency behavior was tested.
What does “ordered” commit us to here?

The relevant order is that the root and free-map generations are flushed before the checksummed inactive manifest is published. That is the ordering being adopted. The decision does not specify an order between every individual root flush and every individual free-map flush, or provide a complete low-level publication protocol.
Why include the free-map flushes in the decision rather than mentioning only the root and manifest?

Because the recovered root must be interpreted consistently with reclamation state. Adopting the root flushes without the associated free-map-generation flushes would leave out the part of the decision concerned with preventing reclaimed records from reappearing after a crash. The adopted ordering links both kinds of state to manifest publication.
Does “checksummed inactive-manifest publication” mean we're treating an 8 MiB manifest write as atomic?

No. It identifies the publication approach being adopted, not a claim that an entire 8 MiB write is inherently atomic. The crash-safety claim is about the recovered outcome at the exercised persistence boundaries. The checksummed manifest and the ordering are parts of that approach; the wording need not assert a hardware-atomic manifest write.
Should I say the manifest alone makes the index crash-safe?

No. The decision is to adopt the combination: ordered root/free-map flushes *and* checksummed inactive-manifest publication. Attributing the result to the manifest alone would omit the required ordering and the reclamation state that goes with the root.
When I say BoundaryCrash-1 verified crash safety, which properties am I talking about?

In this context, crash safety means that recovery did not lose acknowledged commits or resurrect reclaimed records at the injected boundaries BoundaryCrash-1 exercised. It should not be read as a separate claim that the run established serializability or exhausted crashes outside its stated coverage.
Can I call 16 MiB the recovery cost?

You can call it the observed recovery-read bound for BoundaryCrash-1, but “cost” on its own is broader and less precise. The reported figure is at most 16 MiB read per 100 GiB of index; it is not an elapsed-time measurement or a statement that each recovery read exactly 16 MiB.
Does adopting this approach mean recovery will always read exactly the two manifests?

That does not follow from the decision. The 16 MiB figure describes recovery reads in BoundaryCrash-1, not a per-component read trace. The adoption statement need not claim which manifest data was read on any particular recovery.
How does this decision answer the concern about matching a committed root to a free-map generation?

It adopts publication only after the root and free-map generations have been flushed, so the published manifest is intended to identify a coherent recoverable state. BoundaryCrash-1's crash-safety result supports using that approach at the boundaries it exercised. The decision does not require you to claim that a checksum, considered in isolation, establishes the match.
Is the word “adopt” important?

Yes. It makes this a design choice rather than another hypothesis about what might work. You are choosing ordered root/free-map flushes and checksummed inactive-manifest publication. The BoundaryCrash-1 result is the stated basis for that choice, while its measured scope remains the run's injected crashes and recovery reads.
Would it be accurate to say the decision settles the entire transactional-index design?

No. It settles the publication approach named here. The broader index goal also includes serializable concurrency and recovery-read behavior independent of completed transaction count. This decision should not be phrased as though BoundaryCrash-1 separately verified all of those broader properties.
I don't want the qualification to make the decision sound tentative. How can I keep both points clear?

Use decisive wording for the choice and precise wording for the evidence: “Adopt ordered root/free-map flushes followed by checksummed inactive-manifest publication. BoundaryCrash-1 verified preservation of acknowledged commits and non-resurrection of reclaimed records at its injected crash boundaries, with recovery reading at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index.” The adoption is definite; the verification is described within its actual scope.
Could I shorten that to “Adopt the verified manifest protocol”?

That would lose what was adopted: the ordered root/free-map flushes as well as publication of the checksummed inactive manifest. It could also make “verified” sound broader than BoundaryCrash-1's crash-safety result. Naming both parts keeps the decision intelligible without a lengthy explanation.
Should the decision mention historical transaction scanning?

It may be useful context for the publication question, but it is not necessary to state this decision. The decision names the adopted flush and publication approach and cites BoundaryCrash-1's crash-safety verification and recovery reads. It does not add a separate finding about scanning historical transactions or independence from completed transaction count.
Give me one final decision sentence.

Adopt ordered root/free-map flushes followed by checksummed inactive-manifest publication; BoundaryCrash-1 verified crash safety at its injected boundaries with recovery reads of at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB of index.

The next plan is to implement the adopted manifest publication with predicate-version validation and epoch-gated reclamation, then crash-test 10 million transactions against the 64 MiB recovery cap. How should I describe that work?

Describe it as implementation and testing still to be done. The implementation combines the adopted manifest-publication approach with predicate-version validation for serializable concurrency and epoch-gated reclamation for safe record lifetimes. The planned crash test exercises 10 million transactions and checks recovery reads against the cap of 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, alongside the requirement that injected persistence-boundary crashes neither lose acknowledged commits nor resurrect reclaimed records.
What is predicate-version validation meant to contribute?

It is the planned validation component for the concurrency side of the index. Conceptually, a transaction can validate versions associated with the conditions on which its work depended before its outcome is accepted. The implementation still has to define those predicates, their versions, and the checks that make accepted concurrent outcomes serializable; the plan does not claim those rules are already implemented.
Does the word “predicate” specify the layout of the index?

No. It identifies what the validation is about—conditions a transaction relies on—without specifying an index layout or a particular representation of those conditions. The plan names predicate-version validation but leaves its detailed design to the implementation.
Could I say predicate-version validation guarantees serializability?

Not solely from its name. Serializability is the property the validation must deliver. You can say the plan is to implement predicate-version validation for that purpose, then distinguish that intention from a demonstrated guarantee.
Where does that validation meet manifest publication?

The design must connect an accepted, serializable transaction outcome to the state that manifest publication makes recoverable. A transaction should not become an acknowledged commit that recovery can lose, and recovery should not mistake tentative work for an accepted outcome. The plan identifies the components to connect; it does not yet supply every rule governing that connection.
And what does epoch-gated reclamation add?

It is the planned mechanism for controlling when records can be reclaimed, rather than treating removal from a current view as automatically sufficient to reuse their memory. Its rules must protect any use that still depends on a record and remain safe across recovery. The plan does not specify how epochs are represented, advanced, or persisted, so those details should not be presented as settled.
Is epoch-gated reclamation automatically crash-safe?

No. The gate must be consistent with persistent state and with the root and free-map generations that recovery selects. An injected crash must not let recovery interpret an already reclaimed record as live. Epoch gating is the proposed reclamation approach; crash safety remains a property to establish for the integrated implementation.
Should I describe the three components as separate features?

You can give each its own role, but the implementation has to join them. Predicate-version validation concerns which transactions may commit; manifest publication concerns which committed state recovery may select; epoch-gated reclamation concerns when record lifetimes may end safely. A correct outcome requires their decisions to agree before and after a crash.
The plan says “adopted manifest publication.” Do I need to spell out what is being implemented?

For clarity, you can identify it as the ordered root/free-map flushes followed by checksummed inactive-manifest publication. That names the adopted approach the plan depends on. It does not imply that the new integration with predicate-version validation and epoch-gated reclamation has already been implemented or crash-tested.
What does the 10 million figure refer to?

It is the transaction count specified for the planned crash test: 10 million transactions. It is not a reported number of completed transactions, injected crashes, or successful recoveries. Keep the test size distinct from any results the test might eventually produce.
Can I say we're going to run 10 million crashes?
No. The plan says to crash-test 10 million transactions; it does not specify 10 million crashes or a count of injection points. It should retain that distinction.
What exactly is the recovery limit in this plan?

The cap being tested is at most 64 MiB of recovery reads per 100 GiB of index. It is a bound on data read during recovery, not a bound on recovery time. The wider goal also requires the necessary reads to remain independent of the number of completed transactions.
Why exercise so many transactions if the cap is stated per index size?

Transaction count matters because recovery must not come to rely on reading an ever-growing history of completed work. Crash-testing 10 million transactions can exercise that concern while checking the read cap. A run at that one stated transaction count would not, by itself, prove independence from completed transaction count in general.
Should I treat 64 MiB as the expected measurement?

No. It is the cap against which the planned recovery reads will be checked, expressed per 100 GiB of index. The plan provides no measurement from the 10-million-transaction test and does not predict that recovery will read exactly 64 MiB.
Does the plan specify the size of the images for that crash test?

It specifies the transaction count and the recovery cap, but not an image size for this planned test. Keep the cap in its stated form—64 MiB per 100 GiB of index—rather than silently assuming a particular image size.
What should the crash test check besides bytes read?

It should check the index’s stated crash requirements at the injected persistence boundaries: recovery must retain acknowledged commits and must not resurrect reclaimed records. The read check addresses the recovery cap. The plan does not state a particular number or placement of injections, so those should not be reported as though they were already fixed.
Would a byte count under the cap establish the whole design goal?

No. A recovery-read result cannot substitute for preserving acknowledged commits, preventing resurrection, or establishing serializable concurrency. The planned implementation brings those concerns together, and the crash test checks important recovery properties, but its read count alone cannot establish all of them.
Could the test show safe reclamation but still leave validation in question?

Yes. Not observing a resurrected record after the injected crashes would address the reclamation recovery check in those cases. It would not, by itself, show that predicate-version validation makes concurrent outcomes serializable. Those properties need to be assessed on their own terms as well as in the integrated design.
How do I avoid presenting this as a completed experiment?

Use future-facing language: “Implement the adopted manifest publication with predicate-version validation and epoch-gated reclamation, then crash-test 10 million transactions against the recovery-read cap of 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index.” Describe retained acknowledged commits and non-resurrection as conditions the test must check, not as outcomes already observed for this implementation.
Can you give me a fuller plan statement that includes the overall reason for doing it?

Implement the adopted ordered root/free-map flushes and checksummed inactive-manifest publication together with predicate-version validation and epoch-gated reclamation, so the index can address serializable concurrency, crash-safe record lifetimes, and recoverable commits as one design. Then crash-test 10 million transactions: at the injected persistence-boundary crashes, check that acknowledged commits survive and reclaimed records do not reappear, and measure recovery reads against the 64 MiB-per-100 GiB cap. The test is planned; it has not yet supplied results, and the general requirement that recovery reads be independent of completed transaction count remains to be established.

Does this node tell us precisely when each crash is injected?

The activity proposes exercising that interaction; it does not predetermine what will be observed.
What would recovery need to preserve in those tests?

Those are the relevant recovery properties to inspect when crashes are injected during IndexProto-1's transactions. Their satisfaction in this prototype remains to be determined by the activity.
Where does the recovery-read cap enter the picture?

The broader plan calls for crash-testing against a recovery-read cap of 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count. The cap remains a criterion for evaluating recovery, not a measurement from IndexProto-1.
Should I mention 100 GiB images in the IndexProto-1 activity?

Not as a specified size for this activity. Its stated workload is 10 million transactions, with crashes injected during them. You can express the recovery cap in its size-relative form—64 MiB per 100 GiB of index—without asserting that IndexProto-1's images have a particular size.
Is the aim to find out whether completed transaction count forces more recovery reads?

How do I keep the build and crash-injection parts distinct?

State them in sequence: build IndexProto-1 with dual-manifest publication, predicate-version validation, and epoch-gated reclamation; then inject crashes during 10 million transactions. The first clause identifies what is to be implemented. The second identifies how the integrated prototype is to be exercised. Neither clause should be rewritten as an observed outcome.

Any eventual conclusions would need to match what was actually checked: transaction behavior, recovery of acknowledged commits, treatment of reclaimed records, and recovery reads, as applicable.
Can you give me a concise activity statement?

Build IndexProto-1 with dual-manifest publication, predicate-version validation, and epoch-gated reclamation, and inject crashes during 10 million transactions to exercise the integrated transactional and recovery behavior. The build and crash-injection results remain to be reported.

Is the harness part of IndexProto-1, or is it just a proposed external test?

For IndexProto-1, I want to fault it at every flush across 10 million transactions. The checks are serializability, acknowledged commits, absence of freed records, and recovery reads. How should I state this activity?

Does “every flush” mean every transaction gets its own injected crash?

Should I narrow the wording to root, free-map, and manifest flushes?

Not automatically. The activity specifies flush-point faults. A claim about crashes at other points would need its own basis. Describe the coverage as every flush across the stated transaction activity, then report conclusions only for what that activity actually exercises.

It checks the transactional outcomes exercised in this faulted run, including whether the outcomes accepted as committed remain consistent with a serial execution. No. An acknowledged outcome could survive a crash yet still be inconsistent with any serial execution of the concurrent transactions. Conversely, a serializable outcome could be lost during recovery. Keeping both checks is important because they address different properties.
What should the acknowledged-commit check ask at an injected fault?

It should ask whether recovery retains every commit that had already been acknowledged when that fault occurred. The wording must retain “acknowledged”: the activity does not prescribe what happens to a transaction that had not been acknowledged at the fault point.
And how should I express “freed-record absence”?

Ask whether records that were freed remain absent as live records after recovery. This is the reclamation-side check: recovery must not bring a freed record back into the index’s live state. Could preservation of a commit conflict with freed-record absence?

They need to hold for the same recovered state. It would not be enough to preserve acknowledged commits by selecting a state that makes freed records live again, or to keep freed records absent by dropping acknowledged commits. Testing both checks at the flush faults examines that interaction in IndexProto-1.
What about recovery reads—am I just checking whether recovery starts?

No. Recovery reads are an amount to check, not merely an indication that recovery ran. Count the data recovery actually needs to read to establish the recovered state. The design objective is at most 64 MiB of recovery reads per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count; this activity has not supplied a measured value.
Does the activity specify the size of the index used in the run?

It specifies 10 million transactions, not an index size. You can cite the recovery-read criterion in its size-relative form, but should not assume the run uses a 100 GiB image or state an absolute read allowance for an unspecified image size.
Is ten million a result from the test or its intended scale?

It is the stated transaction scale of the faulting activity. The node does not say how many transactions completed, how many faults occurred, or what any check found. Those would be results to report separately.
Should the four checks be evaluated together at each fault?

Can I say that this validates predicate-versioned transactions and epoch-gated free maps?

Whether the run validates either behavior depends on the observations; none are reported in this activity.
Where do copy-on-write roots and dual-manifest commits matter in the test description?

They are part of IndexProto-1’s recoverable commit state. Faulting flushes can exercise the transition between a proposed root and a published committed state, while the recovery checks ask what survives and what remains absent. You need not invent a particular root-selection or manifest-update trace to describe the test.
If recovery stays under the read limit at the tested faults, would that prove independence from transaction count?

A read result from faults across 10 million transactions would establish what was measured for that activity. Independence from completed transaction count is a broader requirement; this node does not specify a comparison across transaction counts or provide measurements. Do not present that broader property as an observed result of a test that has not yet reported outcomes.
Could you give me a results-neutral sentence I can use as the activity description?

Fault IndexProto-1 at every flush across 10 million transactions, and check serializability, preservation of acknowledged commits, absence of freed records after recovery, and recovery reads. The activity specifies the checks and fault points, not their outcomes.

What does zero serializability violations establish in the report?

Can I describe every possible concurrent execution as serializable now?

The precise evidence is zero serializability violations in IndexProto-1’s 10-million-transaction fault run. That is not, by itself, a statement about every possible concurrent execution. Wording the claim as an observation in the run retains its scope.
What does the lost-commit count include?

It is zero *lost acknowledged commits*. The qualifier matters: the finding concerns commits that had been acknowledged, not a claim that every transaction in progress at a fault became committed. The evidence supplies no separate outcome count for unacknowledged transactions.
And does zero resurrected records mean none of the records were ever freed?
No. It means the run found no record that reappeared as live after being reclaimed. It does not give the number of records freed or say that none were freed.
Why list commit preservation and non-resurrection separately if both concern recovery?

They catch different failures. A recovered state might retain acknowledged commits while wrongly reviving a reclaimed record, or keep reclaimed records absent while losing an acknowledged commit. The fault run reports zero findings in each category, so neither needs to stand in for the other.
Should I say the prototype had zero errors overall?

That would be broader than the reported checks. Name the three categories: zero serializability violations, zero lost acknowledged commits, and zero resurrected records. The evidence does not make a claim about every possible kind of error.
How precisely should I express the recovery-read result?

Use “recovery read ≤16 MiB per 100 GiB of index,” or equivalently “at most 16 MiB per 100 GiB.” Retain both the inequality and the size-relative unit. The finding is a read bound, not an exact count for every recovery.
Would “all recoveries read 16 MiB” convey the same thing?
No. The reported upper bound allows recoveries to read less. It gives no individual read counts and does not say that any recovery read exactly 16 MiB.

Can I explain the byte result by saying recovery read only the two manifests?

Not from this finding. It reports how much recovery read, not a trace identifying the data read. Even if two manifests have a combined size that resembles the bound, that resemblance does not establish which data recovery accessed.
Does this run show that recovery reads never grow with the number of completed transactions?

Is the figure an average over recoveries?
No average is given. “≤16 MiB per 100 GiB” is an upper-bound statement. The evidence supplies no distribution of recovery reads, so there is no basis for quoting an average, median, or percentile.
How should I tie the read result to the correctness findings?

Present them as findings from the same IndexProto-1 fault run, but keep their meanings separate: its checks found none of the three named failures, and its recoveries read no more than the stated amount per 100 GiB. Can I say the checks covered every flush in this run without claiming every imaginable crash?

Yes. “Faulted at every flush across 10 million transactions” accurately describes the run’s coverage. It need not be expanded into a claim about crash points other than those flush faults or about executions beyond this run.
Is this a result for the integrated IndexProto-1 rather than an isolated component?

Yes. The evidence identifies IndexProto-1’s fault run. Its findings concern the prototype as exercised during that run: transaction serializability, preservation of acknowledged commits, absence of resurrected records, and recovery reads. The result does not isolate a contribution from any single component.
If I mention predicate-versioned transactions or epoch-gated free maps, should I attribute the zero findings to one of them?

You may identify those as components of IndexProto-1, but this evidence does not isolate causes. It is more accurate to say the integrated prototype produced the stated findings in the run than to assign a particular zero count to a component without further evidence.
