“In IndexProto-1’s fault run at every flush across 10 million transactions, we found zero serializability violations, zero lost acknowledged commits, and zero resurrected records; recovery read ≤16 MiB per 100 GiB of index.”

I have another hypothesis about linking committed roots to free-map generations across crashes: an aligned 8-byte durable selector pointing to an immutable root/free-map capsule permits recovery reads of ≤8 KiB without scanning historical transactions. How should I state it?

State it as a hypothesis, not an established result: an aligned 8-byte durable selector identifies an immutable capsule that binds a root to its associated free-map information, allowing recovery to read no more than 8 KiB without scanning historical transactions. The claim still needs an argument that recovery can recognize the right capsule after a crash and that its read count includes everything needed to do so.
What does the selector contribute to the idea?

It is the proposed small, durable reference from which recovery begins identifying a committed root/free-map combination. Rather than consulting historical transactions to work out which combination belongs together, recovery would follow the selector to a capsule intended to contain that association. The hypothesis does not yet specify the selector’s encoding or how it is updated.
Is the selector itself the committed root?

No. As stated, the selector points to an immutable root/free-map capsule. The capsule is the proposed unit that associates the root with free-map information; the selector identifies that unit. Keeping those roles separate helps explain what recovery would read and what it would infer from those reads.
Why specify that the selector is an aligned 8-byte value?

Alignment and the 8-byte size are explicit parts of the hypothesis’s proposed publication mechanism. They do not, by themselves, prove that a write to the selector is indivisible across every relevant crash or that recovery can always identify a valid value. Those properties, insofar as the hypothesis needs them, require a crash model and a publication argument.
Does “durable selector” imply a particular instruction or flush sequence?

No particular instruction sequence is given. “Durable” expresses what the selector must be for recovery to use it after a crash; the hypothesis does not specify how that durability is achieved. An implementation would have to make the relationship between the selector and the capsule persistently safe, rather than relying on the adjective alone.
What does immutability buy the capsule?

If a capsule remains unchanged after it becomes eligible for recovery, recovery need not interpret an in-progress edit to that capsule as a committed combination. Immutability helps make the root/free-map association a stable object to identify. It does not alone establish when a capsule becomes eligible, whether the selector is safe to follow, or whether the referenced data remains available.
Is the capsule meant to contain an entire root and every free map?

The hypothesis says only that it is an immutable root/free-map capsule; it does not specify its layout or say that all free-map data is physically inside it. What matters to the claim is that recovery can establish the necessary association using no more than 8 KiB of reads. Any information it must read to make that association counts toward the proposed bound.
Could the capsule identify free-map generations indirectly?

That is compatible with the conceptual question, provided the indirect information is sufficient to bind the selected root to the appropriate free-map generations after a crash. The hypothesis does not choose a representation. If recovery must follow additional references to establish the binding, their read cost must still fit within ≤8 KiB.
What does “without history scans” exclude?

It excludes requiring recovery to scan historical transactions to determine the committed root/free-map association. The intended evidence is the durable selector and the immutable capsule it identifies, within the proposed read budget. It does not say historical transactions cannot exist; it says recovering this state must not depend on scanning them.
Does avoiding a history scan automatically prove the 8 KiB bound?

No. Recovery might avoid transaction history yet still need to read more than 8 KiB from other structures. The ≤8 KiB claim applies to recovery reads, not just historical-transaction reads. An evaluation must account for the selector, capsule, and any other data necessary to establish a safe recovered state.
Am I claiming that the selector plus capsule will always fit within 8 KiB?

The stated hypothesis claims recovery can read ≤8 KiB; it does not give component sizes beyond the aligned 8-byte selector. Whether capsule reads and any other required reads fit in the remaining budget is part of what must be established. It would be premature to assert a specific capsule size.
What is the central crash-safety question for publishing the selector?

Whether a crash can leave recovery following a selector to a capsule that is absent, incomplete, or not the committed root/free-map combination. The hypothesis needs a publication rule under which a recoverable selector refers only to a usable immutable capsule, and acknowledgment must remain consistent with whichever state recovery can select. The rule has not been supplied here.
If the capsule is immutable, can I publish the selector before the capsule is durable?

Immutability does not answer that ordering question. If recovery could see the new durable selector without being able to read the capsule it identifies, it could not rely on the proposed association. The hypothesis therefore requires a sound persistence relationship between capsule availability and selector publication, without specifying the operations that establish it.
Does an aligned 8-byte selector automatically provide atomic publication?

No. An 8-byte size and alignment are not, on their own, a proof of atomic durable publication under the crashes being considered. The design would need to show what values recovery may observe if a crash interrupts a selector update and how it recognizes an eligible committed capsule in each case.
Suppose recovery finds a selector value. What must it be able to conclude?

It must be able to conclude that the value identifies a capsule it can safely use, that the capsule binds a committed root to the corresponding free-map state, and that selecting that state will not lose an acknowledged commit or resurrect a reclaimed record. Finding an 8-byte value is only the beginning of that reasoning, not its conclusion.
Why bring acknowledged commits into a hypothesis focused on recovery reads?

Because a very small recovery read count is useful only if it yields the correct committed state. If a crash causes the selector to lead recovery to a state that omits an already acknowledged commit, the recovery-read claim might still hold numerically but the transactional index would fail its durability requirement. The hypothesis must be evaluated against both the byte bound and crash correctness.
And how does the free-map side relate to reclaimed records?

The capsule is proposed to link a selected root with the free-map information appropriate for interpreting that root. That association is relevant to avoiding a post-crash interpretation that brings a reclaimed record back as live. The mere presence of a free-map reference in an immutable capsule would not prove non-resurrection; the meaning and safe use of that reference still matter.
Does this hypothesis change how concurrent transactions are validated?

It makes no such claim. The selector-and-capsule idea addresses publication and recovery of a committed root/free-map association. Serializable concurrent outcomes remain a separate obligation; recovery must faithfully represent accepted outcomes, but this hypothesis does not specify a validation method.
Could recovery read the selector and nothing else?

That would not follow from the hypothesis. It specifically points to an immutable capsule, and recovery may need to read it to establish the root/free-map association. The ≤8 KiB limit is on the necessary recovery reads in total, not a claim that the 8-byte selector alone contains everything recovery needs.
Is the ≤8 KiB limit stated per 100 GiB of index?

Not in this hypothesis. It says ≤8 KiB recovery reads, without a per-index-size qualifier. The broader index requirement is expressed as at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count. Keep those units and scopes distinct rather than silently rewriting the hypothesis as a size-relative measurement.
What would I need to examine at an injected persistence-boundary crash?

Examine the selector value recovery can observe, whether its referenced immutable capsule is available and coherent, and whether the resulting root/free-map association is a state recovery may legitimately select. Then check that acknowledged commits remain present, reclaimed records remain absent, and the reads needed to reach that conclusion are ≤8 KiB without a historical-transaction scan. These are checks the hypothesis calls for, not reported findings.
Could the bound hold for some crashes but not others?

It could; that possibility is why the ≤8 KiB claim needs to be checked at the relevant crash boundaries rather than inferred from the normal recovery path. A boundary that forces additional reads to disambiguate the selector or its capsule would matter, even if other recoveries read less.
What about many completed transactions? Does the hypothesis depend on counting them?

The proposed way of recovering is to use the durable selector and its immutable capsule, not to scan completed transactions. To meet the intended no-history-scan claim over time, those bounded current references would have to remain sufficient no matter how much transaction history has accumulated. The hypothesis states that intended property but supplies no test result or proof of it.
How can I present the idea without implying we've already replaced any publication mechanism?

Present it solely as a hypothesis about a selector-to-capsule recovery path. Say what it predicts—an aligned 8-byte durable selector to an immutable root/free-map capsule permits ≤8 KiB recovery reads without historical transaction scans—and identify the crash-coherence and correctness conditions that would need evaluation. The hypothesis itself is not an adoption decision.
Give me a short, careful statement of the hypothesis and its open obligation.

Hypothesis: an aligned 8-byte durable selector pointing to an immutable root/free-map capsule lets recovery identify a coherent committed state with ≤8 KiB of reads and no historical-transaction scan. It remains to show that selector publication and capsule availability stay crash-safe, and that the recovered state preserves acknowledged commits without resurrecting reclaimed records.

I want to test selector publication in SelectorCrash-1 by crashing at each flush across 10 million transactions. The measurements are recovery bytes and reclamation safety. How should I frame the activity?

Frame SelectorCrash-1 as a test of the selector-publication hypothesis, not as a result. Across 10 million transactions, inject a crash at each flush and examine recovery afterward. How does the immutable capsule enter a recovery-byte measurement?

Does the test plan say that recovery reads only the selector and capsule?

What would the recovery-byte figure be compared against?

The immediate hypothesis being evaluated proposes ≤8 KiB of recovery reads without historical transaction scans. SelectorCrash-1 should measure bytes so that claim can be assessed at its crash points. The broader index goal states a separate recovery-read limit of at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index; neither limit is a measurement from SelectorCrash-1 yet.
Is the ≤8 KiB claim per 100 GiB too?

No. The selector hypothesis states ≤8 KiB recovery reads without a per-index-size qualifier. The 64 MiB limit is the one expressed per 100 GiB of index. Preserve that difference when stating what SelectorCrash-1 measures and what each claim would mean.
Should I assume the SelectorCrash-1 index image is 100 GiB?

No image size is specified for SelectorCrash-1. The activity gives a transaction count and flush-point fault coverage, then calls for recovery-byte and reclamation-safety measurements. You can retain the broader size-relative requirement as context without assigning the test an unstated image size.
What does checking reclamation safety mean here?

Check whether recovery after an injected crash treats a reclaimed record as live again. The test plan does not specify how records are identified for this check or report any outcome.
If recovery reads less than 8 KiB, does that establish reclamation safety?

Conceptually, yes. Recovery might avoid resurrecting records but need more than the hypothesized ≤8 KiB of reads. That would be a different finding for each measure. SelectorCrash-1 has not supplied either finding yet.
What should I look for if a crash happens during selector publication?

The central question is whether recovery can use the persistent selector state it observes to reach a valid root/free-map capsule, rather than interpret an incomplete publication as a safe committed association. For this activity, record how many bytes that recovery requires and whether reclaimed records stay absent. The plan does not predetermine what selector value a particular crash leaves behind.
Can I split the test description into crashes before and after publication?

You can use those as conceptual ways to discuss why flush-point crashes matter, but do not replace the stated injection rule with a narrower schedule. SelectorCrash-1 calls for crashes at each flush across 10 million transactions. Without a specified publication sequence, avoid asserting which flushes are before, during, or after a particular selector update.
Does this activity directly check the no-history-scan part of the hypothesis?

It specifies a measurement of recovery bytes, not a separate trace or classification of every read. A bounded byte count can bear on the proposed no-history-scan recovery path, but the activity as written does not independently report whether recovery consulted historical transactions. Keep that distinction clear when interpreting eventual results.
Does testing 10 million transactions establish that recovery is independent of completed transaction count?

Not by itself. The run exercises flush-point crashes across 10 million transactions, but the activity does not specify a comparison across different completed-transaction counts or provide recovery-read results. Should serializability be listed among the measurements for SelectorCrash-1?

The stated measurements are recovery bytes and reclamation safety. Serializable transaction outcomes remain part of the overall index goal, but adding a serializability measurement to the description of this activity would go beyond what is specified. You can explain that SelectorCrash-1 focuses on selector publication without implying it evaluates every index property.
What about preservation of acknowledged commits?

That remains an essential crash-recovery requirement for the index and a consideration when reasoning about selector publication. But SelectorCrash-1, as stated, specifically calls for measuring recovery bytes and reclamation safety. Would a passing reclamation check prove the capsule always contains the correct free-map generation?

It would show what happened under the tested flush-point crashes and the reclamation check used there. It would not, by itself, specify the capsule contents or prove that every conceivable root/free-map association is correct. At this stage, even a passing result is hypothetical: the activity has not reported observations.
How should I phrase the purpose without promising the ≤8 KiB result?

Say the purpose is to evaluate whether selector publication permits recovery within the hypothesized ≤8 KiB read bound while keeping reclaimed records from reappearing at the exercised crash points. “Evaluate whether” leaves the outcome open. The 10-million-transaction scale and the crash-at-each-flush rule describe how SelectorCrash-1 will exercise the proposal.
Give me a concise, results-neutral test statement.

Run SelectorCrash-1 to test selector publication by injecting a crash at each flush across 10 million transactions; after recovery, measure bytes read and check that reclaimed records have not reappeared. Use those observations to evaluate the ≤8 KiB selector hypothesis, without treating the proposed bound or reclamation safety as an observed result.
SelectorCrash-1 found two stale-pointer resurrections without generation scans. Preventing them required 24 MiB of recovery reads, exceeding 8 KiB. How should I report those findings?

Report both the condition and the read cost: “In SelectorCrash-1, recovery without generation scans produced two stale-pointer resurrections. Preventing those resurrections required 24 MiB of recovery reads, exceeding 8 KiB.” That preserves the distinction between what happened without the scans and what recovery had to read to prevent it.

Neither is specified. It counts the stale-pointer resurrections found in SelectorCrash-1. The finding does not say how many crashes produced them or how many transactions were involved.
Should I describe the two resurrections as happening after different flushes?

No breakdown by flush is reported. SelectorCrash-1 crashed at each flush across 10 million transactions, but this finding does not identify the particular flushes associated with the two resurrections.

Could I say that every recovery without generation scans resurrected a stale pointer?
No. The report identifies two stale-pointer resurrections, not a resurrection in every recovery without generation scans. It provides no total number of recoveries in that condition.

It is the reported amount of recovery reads required to prevent the stale-pointer resurrections. It is not stated as a write volume, a memory footprint, or an elapsed recovery time.
Is 24 MiB an average across the test?
No average is given. The finding says prevention required 24 MiB of recovery reads. It does not provide a distribution of read counts or say that every recovery read exactly 24 MiB.
Can I put “per 100 GiB” after 24 MiB?
Not from this finding. It reports 24 MiB of recovery reads without a per-index-size qualifier. The reported comparison is that 24 MiB exceeds 8 KiB; adding “per 100 GiB” would change the stated unit.

I want to propose a persistent-memory transactional index using strict two-phase predicate locks, shadow-paged roots, and a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory with epoch-quarantined reuse. How do these pieces fit together?

They address different parts of the index goal. Strict two-phase predicate locks are the proposed concurrency mechanism for serializable transactions, including transactions whose reads depend on a range rather than only on records already present. Shadow-paged roots are the proposed way to distinguish a committed index view from a view being updated. The 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory and epoch-quarantined reuse address allocation and record lifetimes across crashes. The proposal still needs rules connecting all four: recovery must preserve acknowledged commits, must not resurrect reclaimed records, and must read at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index independently of completed transaction count.
What does “strict two-phase” add to predicate locking?

It proposes that locks protecting a transaction’s relevant reads and writes remain held through its commit or abort decision, rather than being released while the transaction could still affect concurrent outcomes. Predicate locks extend that protection to conditions such as a key range, including qualifying records that might be inserted later. Those are the intended concurrency semantics; the proposal does not yet specify the lock representation or acquisition rules.
Why lock a predicate instead of only locking the records a scan returned?

A transaction can depend on there being no additional qualifying record in a scanned range. Locking only returned records would not express that dependency when another transaction tries to insert a qualifying record—or when the scan returns nothing. Predicate locking is proposed to cover the condition the transaction observed, not just the particular records it found.
Does naming predicate locks prove the index is serializable?

No. The locks must cover all relevant transaction dependencies, and conflicting operations must respect them through the required transaction boundary. Strict two-phase predicate locking is the proposed route to serializability; its name alone does not establish that a particular implementation covers every predicate or correctly handles concurrent operations.
What is the job of the shadow-paged roots?

Their proposed job is to provide a recoverable distinction between an existing committed view and an updated view. Recovery should be able to identify a valid committed root without accepting a partially completed update as committed. Shadow paging describes that general approach, but this proposal does not specify the root-publication operation or the persistence ordering needed to make it safe across crashes.
Is a root becoming visible the same as a commit being acknowledged?

Not by definition. The design needs an explicit relationship among the transaction’s commit decision, publication of its recoverable root, and acknowledgment. Once a commit is acknowledged, an injected persistence-boundary crash must not cause recovery to lose it. Simply finding a root after a crash would not establish whether it represents an acknowledged commit.
What does the allocation directory contribute?

It is the proposed bounded directory for allocation state, maintained in double-buffered form. Recovery needs a sound way to interpret that state alongside the selected root so that record reuse cannot make reclaimed records appear live again. The proposal specifies a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory, but not its fields, publication rule, or the precise reads recovery will require.
Should I describe that as two 16 MiB directories?

The wording here is “a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory.” It does not explicitly say whether 16 MiB describes the whole double-buffered directory or each buffer. Keep the given description rather than assigning an unstated size to each copy.
Does double buffering make updates to the directory atomic?

Not on its own. Double buffering offers a way to retain candidate directory states while one is being changed, but the design must define how a state becomes eligible for recovery and how an interrupted update is recognized. Recovery must not combine allocation information from one state with an incompatible committed root.
Why is it important to match the directory to the root?

The root says which index view recovery is using; allocation state bears on which storage locations can be treated as occupied, reclaimed, or reusable. If recovery selected them independently without a coherent relationship, it could preserve an index view while misinterpreting a record’s lifetime. A valid recovered state must retain acknowledged commits and exclude reclaimed records at the same time.
What does “epoch-quarantined reuse” mean at the proposal level?

It proposes delaying reuse of a location after reclamation until an epoch-based condition permits reuse. Quarantine is intended to keep an old reference from being confused with a later use of the same location. The proposal does not define epoch advancement, what evidence makes reuse permissible, or how those decisions persist across crashes.
Is quarantine itself the same as reclamation?

They are related but not identical ideas. Quarantine concerns when storage associated with a reclaimed record becomes eligible for reuse. The no-resurrection requirement concerns whether recovery could treat a reclaimed record as live. The proposed epoch rule has to support that safety property even if a crash interrupts a transition involving the directory, root, or reuse eligibility.
Could we keep a location quarantined indefinitely and call the crash-safety question solved?

Keeping a location unavailable for reuse could avoid one kind of premature reuse, but it would not by itself establish that recovery never revives a reclaimed record or that acknowledged commits survive. The proposal specifically includes epoch-quarantined *reuse*, so it needs safe rules both for quarantine and for eventually allowing reuse. No timing or capacity policy for that transition is specified here.
What must be true if a crash occurs while allocation state is changing?

Recovery must select an allocation state it can safely interpret with the committed root it selects. It must not interpret an incomplete directory change as permission to revive a reclaimed record or lose an acknowledged commit. The proposed double buffering is relevant to that question, but the exact selection and publication rules remain to be defined.
And if a crash happens while a shadow-paged root is being published?

The same overall obligations apply: recovery must identify a valid committed view, preserve every commit acknowledged before the crash, and avoid resurrecting reclaimed records. It cannot rely solely on whether the proposed new root exists somewhere in persistent memory. Publication must distinguish an eligible committed root from incomplete work and relate it to safe allocation state.
Can strict two-phase locks solve those crash questions?

No. They address concurrency among running transactions, not what persistent state remains interpretable after a crash. Conversely, a crash-safe root and directory would not by themselves show that concurrent transactions were serializable. The proposal needs both a concurrency argument and a persistence-and-reclamation argument.
How does this proposal aim to avoid recovery work proportional to the index?

The bounded allocation directory is a proposed place for recovery to obtain allocation information without scanning the entire index. A recoverable root likewise offers a way to locate a committed view without examining every index entry. That is an intended architecture, not yet a demonstrated recovery bound: any additional data recovery must read to establish correctness counts toward the limit.
Can I conclude recovery reads 16 MiB because the directory is 16 MiB?

No. The directory’s stated size is not a measurement of recovery reads. Recovery might need to read root-publication information or other state, and the double-buffered layout and required reads have not been specified. The complete recovery procedure must be accounted for against at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index.
What about independence from the number of completed transactions?

Recovery cannot require reading an ever-growing completed-transaction history merely to decide which root and allocation state are valid. The proposal should explain how its current recoverable state remains sufficient as transactions accumulate. A 16 MiB directory alone does not prove that independence if recovery also needs to consult history elsewhere.
Is the 64 MiB cap a budget for lock acquisition or transaction validation?

No. It is a recovery-read limit: at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count. The proposal does not give a numerical runtime budget for acquiring predicate locks or for processing individual transactions.
Would a directory state that avoids resurrection be acceptable if it drops the newest acknowledged root?

No. Both requirements must hold in the same recovered state. Avoiding resurrection cannot excuse losing an acknowledged commit, just as preserving an acknowledged commit cannot excuse making a reclaimed record live. Root publication, directory selection, and the acknowledgment rule must be consistent across injected persistence-boundary crashes.
What should we ask about a transaction that removes a record?

Ask how its serializable commit decision relates to the root that represents the resulting index view, how the directory represents the record’s lifetime, and when epoch quarantine permits its storage to be reused. After a crash, recovery must not revive the reclaimed record or lose an acknowledged commit. Those are questions for the proposed protocol; this proposal does not specify the sequence of operations.
Could a read-only range transaction matter to this design even if it never changes a root?

Yes, for the concurrency argument. Its result can depend on a predicate, including the absence of qualifying records, so concurrent changes must respect the relevant predicate locks if its outcome is to be serializable. That does not imply the proposal has specified how read-only transactions are recorded or recovered.

Name it explicitly as a proposal: use strict two-phase predicate locks for serializable concurrency, shadow-paged roots for recoverable index views, and a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory with epoch-quarantined reuse for allocation and reclamation. Then state the obligations still to show: after every injected persistence-boundary crash, acknowledged commits survive and reclaimed records do not reappear; recovery reads at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count.
What's the most important integration question?

Whether each state recovery may select combines a legitimately committed root with allocation and epoch state that is safe for interpreting its records—and whether that state includes every acknowledged commit. The locking rules must establish serializable outcomes before those outcomes are acknowledged and made recoverable. Defining those connections, rather than merely listing the mechanisms, is what would turn the proposal into a complete design.
How can the bounded allocation directory track epoch-quarantined reuse through sustained churn without replaying completed transactions?

The central question is what *current* durable state the directory must retain so recovery can decide which locations are allocated, which remain quarantined, and which may safely be reused. Under sustained churn, completed transactions can keep accumulating even when the index does not grow. If answering those questions requires replaying each completed transaction, recovery reads would depend on transaction count. The proposed 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory needs a way to represent the relevant record-lifetime state within a bounded recovery path; the proposal has not yet specified how.
Why is sustained churn particularly challenging if the index size stays about the same?

Because the same storage can pass through many lifetimes. Index size alone would not tell recovery which lifetime a reference belongs to or whether a freed location is still quarantined. The question asks how to preserve those distinctions as reuse continues, without making recovery reconstruct them from an ever-growing sequence of completed transactions. It does not provide a churn rate or a measured limit on the number of lifetimes.
Wouldn't a bounded directory necessarily forget some earlier transactions?

It need not retain every completed transaction as an individual historical event, but it cannot forget a fact that remains necessary to interpret current roots or decide whether reuse is safe. The design challenge is to distinguish history that can be safely represented by current state from information whose loss would let an old reference appear valid. Merely declaring the directory bounded does not establish that the remaining information is sufficient.
So what must an entry or state in the directory tell recovery?

At the level of this question, it must let recovery establish the allocation and quarantine decisions relevant to the selected committed root. In particular, recovery must not turn a reclaimed record back into a live one or mistake storage that is still quarantined for storage safe to reuse. The question does not specify directory entries or say whether those facts appear directly or through bounded references.
Can I describe the directory as a compact summary of all past allocation decisions?

You can call it a bounded representation of the *currently relevant* allocation and reuse state. Saying it is a summary of all past decisions might imply that every historical decision remains individually recoverable, which is not required by the question. The important property is that recovery can make safe decisions without replaying completed transactions, even after sustained churn.
What does the epoch add to that current-state question?

Epoch quarantine makes reuse conditional rather than immediate. Recovery must be able to determine whether the condition for leaving quarantine has actually been satisfied for a location it might reuse. If a crash makes that determination ambiguous, the directory and recovery rules must not resolve the ambiguity by treating unsafe reuse as safe. The exact epoch rule and its persistent representation remain unspecified.
Could recovery simply assume every quarantined location has become reusable?

Not without a rule showing that assumption is safe at every injected persistence-boundary crash. A location can be reclaimed without yet being eligible for reuse under an epoch-quarantined scheme. Erasing that distinction could undermine the intended protection against confusing a stale reference with a later lifetime.
What if recovery treats every uncertain location as still quarantined?

That is a conceivable conservative response to uncertainty, but it is not a complete solution to the question. The design would still need to specify how quarantine state is represented, how safe reuse eventually becomes possible under sustained churn, and whether its recovery procedure remains within the read bound. The proposal does not choose such a policy.
Is this primarily a capacity question or a crash-safety question?

Both. A bounded directory needs enough capacity to represent the state that continues to matter as records cycle through reclamation and reuse. Its publication and interpretation must also remain crash-safe. A representation that fits but loses necessary lifetime distinctions is unsafe; a correct representation that requires replaying completed transactions to recover does not answer the bounded-recovery question.
How does double buffering affect this problem?

Double buffering is relevant to changing the directory while retaining a candidate state recovery could select. It does not by itself say which candidate is valid after a crash, whether it agrees with the committed root, or whether its quarantine information is current enough to permit reuse. Those selection and consistency rules matter especially when a crash interrupts an update under churn.
Can I assume each of the two directory buffers is 16 MiB?

No. The proposal says “a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory” without specifying whether 16 MiB is the total size or the size of each buffer. The question is about whether that bounded directory can represent the needed state; assigning a size to each buffer would add an unstated detail.
What has to be linked when a shadow-paged root and the directory both change?

Recovery must select a committed root together with allocation and quarantine state that can safely interpret that root. It cannot independently choose a root reflecting one state and a directory reflecting an incompatible reuse decision. It must also retain every acknowledged commit. The question asks how to keep that relationship recoverable without consulting a growing history of completed transactions.
Suppose a record is removed and its location later reused. What would recovery need to distinguish?

It would need to avoid treating a reference to the reclaimed record as a reference to a live record, whether at the old lifetime or after reuse. It would also need a safe basis for deciding that reuse was permitted under the epoch quarantine. That is a conceptual illustration of the lifetime distinction; it does not prescribe an identifier format, a reuse schedule, or a directory layout.
Could a snapshot of the directory eliminate transaction replay?

A current durable representation could avoid replay if it contains all information recovery needs about the selected state and pending quarantine decisions. But calling something a snapshot does not prove it is complete, coherent with the selected root, or bounded as churn continues. The open question is precisely how such a representation remains sufficient after repeated changes.
What does “without replaying completed transactions” rule out exactly?

It rules out requiring recovery to walk a transaction-by-transaction history of completed work in order to reconstruct current allocation and epoch-quarantine state. The transactions may have existed and affected the directory during normal operation; the question is whether recovery can use bounded current evidence instead of reprocessing their accumulated history.
Would replaying only a short recent tail answer the question?

That depends on whether the amount recovery must read remains bounded independently of completed transaction count, and whether the current directory and any such tail together resolve every relevant lifetime safely. The question specifies no tail or replay mechanism, so it would be a design option to justify, not something already supplied by the proposal. Calling a tail “short” would not establish the bound.
Does it matter whether the transaction count grows much faster than the index?

Yes; that is the pressure expressed by sustained churn. Many allocation and reuse transitions could occur without comparable index growth. Recovery is limited to at most 64 MiB of reads per 100 GiB of index, independent of the number of completed transactions. An account that works only while the transaction history remains small would leave the question unanswered.
Is the 16 MiB directory itself enough to claim recovery reads of 16 MiB?

No. The directory’s stated size is not the complete recovery-read measurement. Selecting a committed shadow-paged root and determining which directory state is valid might require other reads, and any such required reads count toward the 64 MiB-per-100 GiB recovery limit. Nor does the 16 MiB description tell us which portions of the double-buffered directory recovery must actually read.
Could recovery defer checking some allocation information until it touches a location?

That is a possible conceptual distinction between what recovery establishes immediately and what it can safely resolve later. The design would need to show that it does not make an unsafe allocation or record-liveness decision before the deferred information is checked. Deferring a necessary read does not by itself demonstrate that recovery has finished safely within its byte budget.
How would a crash during release from quarantine affect the question?

It makes the boundary between still-quarantined and reusable state important. After that crash, recovery must not infer permission to reuse from an incomplete persistent transition. At the same time, the root and directory it selects must preserve acknowledged commits and avoid resurrecting reclaimed records. No particular release sequence is specified, so the requirement is to define and check the safe interpretations at those crash boundaries.
What about a crash after reuse has begun?

Recovery still needs an unambiguous way to interpret the location’s relevant lifetime in the committed state. It must not bring an earlier reclaimed record back as live or lose an acknowledged commit associated with the recoverable root. The directory’s durable allocation and quarantine information must be sufficient to make that interpretation without replaying all completed transactions.
Do strict two-phase predicate locks help decide whether a location is reusable after recovery?

They serve the concurrency side of the proposal, protecting transactional predicates through the commit or abort decision. They do not, merely by being strict two-phase locks, provide durable evidence of a location’s allocation or quarantine state after a crash. The directory, epoch rules, root publication, and acknowledgment boundary need their own persistent consistency argument.
Is there a simple invariant that captures the directory's job during churn?

A useful design obligation is that every state recovery may select contains enough bounded, durable information to interpret the selected committed root’s record lifetimes and to distinguish locations still quarantined from those safe to reuse. The information must remain sufficient regardless of how many transactions have completed. This states what the directory and its associated state need to achieve; it does not assert a specific invariant has already been implemented.
How would I know if a proposed directory scheme fails that obligation?

Look for a state after an injected persistence-boundary crash in which recovery cannot determine whether a location is safe without replaying an accumulated transaction history, or makes a decision that resurrects a reclaimed record. Requiring reads above 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index would also fail the recovery constraint. These are criteria for evaluating a proposed scheme, not findings about this one.
Could the directory meet the read cap while still mishandling an old reference?

Yes. Bounded reads establish only how much recovery consulted, not whether its interpretation was safe. A scheme could read very little and still make a stale reference appear live. Conversely, a safe interpretation that requires replay proportional to completed transactions would fail the recovery-independence condition.
How should I put the unresolved design question in one paragraph?

How can a 16 MiB double-buffered allocation directory retain enough durable information about allocation, epoch quarantine, and permitted reuse through sustained churn that recovery can select it consistently with a committed shadow-paged root? The answer must avoid replaying completed transactions, preserve acknowledged commits, prevent reclaimed records from reappearing after every injected persistence-boundary crash, and keep recovery reads at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index independently of completed transaction count. The directory representation and the rules that would establish those properties remain open.

I have a hypothesis for handling epoch-quarantined reuse through sustained churn: publishing quarantine-ring checkpoints with shadow roots before slot reuse should keep recovery reads at ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB after 100 million transactions. How should I frame it?

Frame it as a prediction to test, not a measured result. The proposed ordering is to publish quarantine-ring checkpoints with shadow roots before slot reuse. The predicted recovery-read bound is ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB of index after 100 million transactions. To answer the underlying churn question, the design would also need to show that recovery can use that bounded published state without replaying completed transactions, while interpreting reuse safely after a crash.
What is the checkpoint supposed to accomplish conceptually?

It is meant to give recovery a current, durable account of quarantine state relevant to slot reuse. If recovery can obtain the necessary account from published checkpoints associated with shadow roots, it need not reconstruct every allocation transition by replaying completed transactions. The hypothesis does not specify the checkpoint’s contents, format, or publication frequency.
Why publish it with a shadow root?

A recovered root and the quarantine state used to interpret its record lifetimes need to agree. Publishing a quarantine-ring checkpoint with a shadow root is intended to make that association recoverable as a coherent state. The wording does not, by itself, establish how recovery identifies a matching pair or rejects an interrupted publication.
Does “with” mean both objects are written atomically?

No. It expresses the intended association, not a claim of a single atomic write. A crash-safety argument would have to identify which root-and-checkpoint combinations recovery may select at each injected persistence boundary and show that none permits unsafe reuse or loses an acknowledged commit.
Why does publication have to happen before slot reuse?

The proposed order aims to avoid reuse becoming visible without durable information needed to interpret the slot’s quarantine status. If a crash occurs around reuse, recovery needs a safe account of whether the slot could be reused and how it relates to the selected root. Publishing first is the hypothesis’s proposed way to supply that account; whether it succeeds remains to be shown.
Can I say the checkpoint gives immediate permission to reuse every quarantined slot?

No. The hypothesis says checkpoints are published before slot reuse; it does not define which slots qualify for reuse or what epoch condition grants permission. A checkpoint could be relevant to deciding that question, but its mere publication is not specified as blanket permission to reuse quarantined slots.
Does the phrase require a new checkpoint for each individual slot?

It does not state a one-checkpoint-per-slot rule. It specifies an ordering between publication of quarantine-ring checkpoints with shadow roots and slot reuse. The checkpoint cadence and the number of slots represented by a checkpoint are open details; assigning either a value would add to the hypothesis.
What does “quarantine ring” tell us about its structure?

It names the quarantine-state structure being checkpointed, but the hypothesis supplies no capacity, entry format, wraparound rule, or epoch layout. The key question is whether its published checkpoints retain the information recovery needs through sustained churn without requiring reads proportional to completed transactions.
Why specify 100 million transactions?

That is the scale at which the hypothesis predicts the read bound will hold. It makes sustained churn concrete without saying how many slots are reclaimed or reused, how many checkpoints are published, or how large the index images are. It is a transaction count, not a crash count or a reported experiment.
Does “after 100 million transactions” mean all 100 million completed?

The hypothesis states “after 100 million transactions” without giving a separate breakdown of attempted, completed, or acknowledged transactions. Keep that wording rather than supplying an unstated breakdown. The broader requirement about independence from completed transaction count would still need its own argument.
If recovery reads no more than the bound at that point, has independence from completed transaction count been proven?

Not by that observation alone. A bound after 100 million transactions would address the stated scale, but independence from completed transaction count is a more general property. The design must explain why additional completed transactions do not force recovery to read an accumulating history or otherwise exceed the applicable read bound.
How should I express the numerical target exactly?

Use “recovery reads ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB of index after 100 million transactions.” Both the inequality and “per 100 GiB” matter. The hypothesis is neither an exact claim that every recovery reads 32 MiB nor an unqualified 32 MiB limit at every index size.
Is 32 MiB the size of the checkpoint?

No checkpoint size is specified. The ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB figure is a proposed bound on recovery reads. Recovery might need to read more than the checkpoint alone to select a shadow root and interpret quarantine state, and those required reads would count toward the bound.
Would it be enough to count only reads of the quarantine ring?

No. If recovery must read root-publication information, checkpoints, directory state, or any other data to establish a safe recovered state, all those reads are part of recovery. Limiting one component’s reads would not establish the hypothesis’s bound on recovery reads as a whole.
How does the 32 MiB figure relate to the index’s 64 MiB recovery cap?

Both are expressed per 100 GiB of index. The hypothesis predicts a ≤32 MiB recovery-read figure after 100 million transactions, while the index goal sets a cap of 64 MiB per 100 GiB, independent of completed transaction count. The prediction is numerically below that cap at the stated scale, but it is not yet a measurement or a proof of the general requirement.
Is the prediction about recovery time as well?
No. MiB per 100 GiB is a read-volume measure. The hypothesis does not specify elapsed recovery time or computational work, so neither should be inferred from the read bound.
Where does the bounded allocation directory fit in this question?

The checkpoints are being proposed to help keep allocation and epoch-quarantine state recoverable under churn. They need to be interpreted consistently with the bounded directory and the selected shadow root. The hypothesis does not say exactly what is stored in the directory versus a checkpoint, or what portion of either recovery reads.
What if a crash occurs after checkpoint publication but before reuse?

Recovery must interpret the published checkpoint and selected root without treating a slot as reused merely because publication occurred. The hypothesis does not prescribe the exact recovered state at that boundary. It must be safe with respect to acknowledged commits and reclaimed records, and its required reads must stay within the proposed bound.
And what if the crash happens during checkpoint publication?

Then recovery needs a rule for recognizing a usable published root-and-checkpoint state rather than mixing incomplete checkpoint information with an incompatible root. The ordering claim alone does not say how an interrupted publication is recognized. This crash boundary is part of what a test or proof would need to examine.
What about a crash once a slot has been reused?

Recovery must still distinguish the slot’s current lifetime from a reclaimed one and select root and quarantine information that justify that interpretation. It must not bring a reclaimed record back as live or lose an acknowledged commit. The hypothesis proposes an ordering relevant to those obligations, but it does not report that they hold at this boundary.
Could a checkpoint be coherent with a shadow root but still allow a stale reference to appear valid?

Yes, unless the contents and interpretation of the checkpoint provide the necessary lifetime distinctions. Coherent publication is one obligation; safe interpretation of reclaimed and reused slots is another. The hypothesis needs both if its approach is to support crash-safe reclamation.
Could recovery be correct but exceed 32 MiB per 100 GiB?

Yes. It might preserve acknowledged commits and avoid resurrecting records yet need more reads to determine safe quarantine and reuse state. That would leave the proposed ≤32 MiB-per-100 GiB prediction unmet, even though the correctness properties held in that case.
What would directly contradict the read prediction?

At the stated 100-million-transaction scale, a recovery that requires more than 32 MiB of reads per 100 GiB of index would contradict the numerical prediction. The figure must include all reads required to establish the recovered state, not only the reads of checkpoint data.
What would directly challenge the proposed reuse ordering as a safety mechanism?

An injected persistence-boundary crash in which recovery resurrects a reclaimed record, permits reuse without the required quarantine state, or loses an acknowledged commit would challenge the safety argument for that ordering. Those are potential failure criteria, not observations supplied by the hypothesis.
Can we say this hypothesis eliminates transaction replay?

Say it aims to answer the question of recovery without replaying completed transactions. The checkpoint approach suggests using bounded current state instead of reconstructing a transaction-by-transaction history, but the hypothesis does not yet show that the checkpoints remain sufficient after sustained churn. Avoid stating the absence of replay as an established result.
What's a careful one-paragraph version?

Hypothesis: publishing quarantine-ring checkpoints together with shadow roots before slot reuse should allow recovery to read ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB of index after 100 million transactions. The approach is intended to keep epoch-quarantine and reuse state recoverable under churn without replaying completed transactions. It remains to establish how recovery selects a coherent root and checkpoint across crashes, whether reclaimed records stay absent and acknowledged commits survive, and whether all necessary recovery reads meet the predicted bound.

I want to extend the PhantomSplit-1 schedules to 100 million split/delete/reuse transactions. The activity would crash at checkpoint and reuse flushes, then check for resurrection and whether recovery reads stay at or below 32 MiB. How should I state it?

State it as an activity to perform: extend the PhantomSplit-1 schedules across 100 million split/delete/reuse transactions, inject crashes at checkpoint flushes and reuse flushes, and after recovery check whether any reclaimed record is resurrected and whether recovery reads are ≤32 MiB. Those are the specified workload, fault points, and checks—not findings from the extended run.
Does 100 million count transactions, or the total number of splits, deletions, and reuses?
It counts transactions in the extended split/delete/reuse activity. It does not give a separate count of splits, deletions, or reuses, nor does it say that each transaction performs all three.
Can I call it 100 million crash tests?
No. The activity specifies 100 million transactions, with crashes injected at checkpoint and reuse flushes. It does not give the number of flushes or injected crashes.
What does extending the PhantomSplit-1 schedules convey?

It identifies the schedules being extended, rather than naming an unrelated test. The extension brings split, delete, and reuse transactions into the stated 100-million-transaction activity. It does not specify a new worker count, a schedule format, or a result for the extended schedules.
Why include deletion and reuse alongside splits?

They make the record-lifetime question observable in the scheduled activity. Deletion and subsequent reuse are relevant to whether recovery could mistake a reclaimed record for a live one, while splits remain part of the transaction mix being exercised. The activity does not say how often those operations occur or prescribe their ordering within a transaction.
What exactly is the checkpoint flush fault point?

It is a flush associated with checkpoint state at which the activity calls for an injected crash. The test description does not specify the checkpoint’s representation, the number of such flushes, or what persistent state each one leaves behind. Recovery after each injected crash is what the stated checks evaluate.
And what qualifies as a reuse flush?

The activity names flushes associated with reuse as the other crash points. It does not define their internal operations or say how many occur. You can retain the term “reuse flush” without assigning it a more detailed persistence sequence than the activity provides.
Am I crashing at every flush in the extended run?

The stated fault points are checkpoint and reuse flushes. Do not broaden that to every flush of every kind. If you want to describe coverage precisely, say that crashes are injected at the checkpoint and reuse flushes exercised by the extended schedules.
Why check recovery after those flushes instead of just observing whether the run completes?

The question being tested concerns persistent state at boundaries around checkpoints and reuse. An uninterrupted run cannot show how recovery interprets that state when a crash interrupts it. Injecting crashes at the named flushes lets the activity check for record resurrection and account for recovery reads at those points; it does not predetermine either result.
What would count as resurrection in this check?

A record that was reclaimed appearing as live after recovery would be a resurrection. The check is about the recovered interpretation of record lifetimes, not merely whether a location has been used more than once. The activity does not specify the checking procedure or report a count.
If a location is reused, is that automatically a resurrection?

No. Reuse and resurrection are different. The concern is whether recovery treats a reclaimed record as live when interpreting the state left by a crash. Reusing a location does not, by itself, establish that the earlier record has reappeared.
Should I check for resurrection only after reuse flushes?

No. The stated check accompanies crashes at both checkpoint and reuse flushes. A checkpoint-related crash can also leave persistent state that recovery must interpret safely. Keep both classes of fault point within the resurrection check.
Is the 32 MiB figure a target or a result?

It is the recovery-read threshold to check in this activity. The extended run has not reported recovery-byte measurements, so write “check recovery reads against ≤32 MiB,” not “recovery read ≤32 MiB.”
Do I measure just checkpoint reads against 32 MiB?

No. The activity says to check recovery, so the relevant quantity is the data recovery needs to read, including any information beyond a checkpoint that is necessary to establish its state. Counting only checkpoint reads would not test a limit on recovery reads.
Does the activity specify that 32 MiB is an average?
No. “≤32 MiB recovery” expresses a ceiling to check, not an average or a prediction that each recovery reads exactly 32 MiB. The activity supplies no measured distribution.
Should I add “per 100 GiB” after 32 MiB in the activity sentence?

The activity itself states a check against ≤32 MiB recovery without an index-size qualifier. Keep that wording when describing this test. If discussing a separate size-relative hypothesis, label its units separately rather than silently changing this activity’s threshold; no index image size is specified here.
Does this extension test whether every acknowledged commit survives?

The checks explicitly named for this activity are resurrection and ≤32 MiB recovery reads. Preservation of acknowledged commits remains an overall index requirement, but the activity statement does not say this extension measures it. Do not report it as a check or result of this activity without that additional information.
What about comparing the extended histories against a serializability oracle?

That is not among the checks stated for this extension. Referring to PhantomSplit-1 identifies the schedules being extended; it does not automatically add an oracle comparison to the checkpoint-and-reuse crash activity. Here, describe the two specified checks rather than implying a new serializability finding.
Does running 100 million transactions prove the recovery-read requirement is independent of completed transaction count?

Not by itself. The extension tests at a stated transaction scale and measures recovery at its specified fault points. Independence from completed transaction count is a broader property; a transaction count alone, even 100 million, does not establish how reads behave at every count.
How would the two checks be interpreted if they disagree?

Keep them separate. A recovery could avoid resurrecting reclaimed records yet read more than 32 MiB, or stay within 32 MiB while resurrecting a record. The activity requires checking both; a favorable result for one cannot substitute for the other. Neither outcome has been reported.
Can I say checkpoint publication makes reuse safe in the test description?

Say the activity *tests* recovery around checkpoint and reuse flushes. Whether checkpoint publication suffices to keep reuse safe is what the resurrection check is meant to help evaluate. Presenting safety as already established would turn the proposed activity into an unsupported result.
Give me a concise, results-neutral statement.

Extend the PhantomSplit-1 schedules to 100 million split/delete/reuse transactions; inject crashes at checkpoint and reuse flushes, then check for resurrected records and whether recovery reads are ≤32 MiB.

The extended PhantomSplit-1 run completed 100 million transactions. It yielded zero resurrected records and zero lost acknowledged commits, and worst-case recovery read 32 MiB per 100 GiB. How should I report the evidence?

“In the extended PhantomSplit-1 run, 100 million transactions yielded zero resurrected records and zero lost acknowledged commits; worst-case recovery read 32 MiB per 100 GiB of index.” That retains the transaction scale, the two zero findings, and the worst-case qualification on the recovery-read figure.
Does 100 million refer to crashes?
No. It refers to transactions. The reported evidence does not give a number of injected crashes, even though the extended activity included crashes at checkpoint and reuse flushes.
Should I identify the transaction mix?

You can describe the extended activity as involving split/delete/reuse transactions. Keep that as the stated transaction mix, without inventing separate counts for splits, deletes, or reuses. The result reports 100 million transactions in total.
Can I say there were 100 million reuse operations?
No. The 100 million figure counts transactions, not reuse operations. The evidence does not specify how many slots were reused or how many transactions included a reuse.
What does zero resurrections mean in this run?

It means the extended PhantomSplit-1 run found no reclaimed record that reappeared as live after recovery at its exercised crash points. It does not give a number of reclaimed records or imply that no records were deleted or reused.
And why keep “acknowledged” when talking about lost commits?

Because the result is zero *lost acknowledged commits*. It does not give the outcome of every transaction that might have been in progress or unacknowledged at a crash. Dropping the qualifier would broaden the reported finding.
Could I combine those as “no crash-related errors”?

That would be less precise and potentially broader. The evidence names two categories: no resurrected records and no lost acknowledged commits. Report both directly rather than implying every possible crash-related property was measured.
What does “worst-case recovery read 32 MiB per 100 GiB” tell me?

It reports the highest recovery-read figure in the extended run as 32 MiB for each 100 GiB of index, using the stated size-relative unit. It is not an average or a claim that every recovery read exactly 32 MiB.
Can I shorten that to “recovery read 32 MiB”?
That would lose both “worst-case” and “per 100 GiB,” changing the meaning. Keep the full phrase so the figure remains an upper-end observation normalized by index size.
Does the result report elapsed recovery time?
No. MiB per 100 GiB describes read volume relative to index size. The finding does not state recovery latency or computation time.
Should I call 32 MiB per 100 GiB the average across all crashes?
No. It is explicitly a worst-case recovery-read figure. No average, median, or distribution is reported.
Does the read figure tell us exactly which structures recovery read?

No. The evidence gives a worst-case total recovery-read figure, not a per-structure breakdown. Do not assign particular portions of the 32 MiB to checkpoints, roots, the allocation directory, or other data without a reported breakdown.
Can I say the result proves recovery never replays completed transactions?

The evidence reports zero resurrections and lost acknowledged commits and the worst-case read figure for this extended run. It does not provide a recovery trace or an explicit finding about transaction replay. Keep any statement about replay tied to what has actually been shown, rather than inferring it solely from the byte total.
Does the 100-million-transaction result prove recovery reads are independent of completed transaction count?

It shows the reported worst-case recovery reads at that stated transaction scale. It does not, on its own, give measurements across transaction counts or a general proof of independence. The accurate claim is the 32 MiB-per-100 GiB worst case observed in the extended run.
How does that compare numerically to the 64 MiB per 100 GiB recovery cap?

The reported worst case of 32 MiB per 100 GiB is below the cap of 64 MiB per 100 GiB at the same index-size basis. That comparison is numerical; it does not turn the extended run into an exhaustive guarantee for every possible workload or crash.
Does it also meet the proposed ≤32 MiB per 100 GiB figure?

For the extended run, a worst-case recovery read of 32 MiB per 100 GiB is at the proposed ≤32 MiB-per-100 GiB boundary. That states how the observed number relates to the predicted threshold for this run, without claiming a general result outside it.
Is the finding about serializability too?

No new serializability finding is stated for the extended run. Its reported outcomes are zero resurrected records, zero lost acknowledged commits, and worst-case recovery reads of 32 MiB per 100 GiB across 100 million transactions. Do not add an oracle result to this evidence.
Can I say every possible checkpoint and reuse crash was covered?

The activity injected crashes at checkpoint and reuse flushes in the extended schedules. The evidence applies to that exercised run. It does not state exhaustive coverage of all possible executions or crash points beyond those schedules.
If I mention the fault points, what's a careful formulation?

“In the extended PhantomSplit-1 schedules, crashes were injected at checkpoint and reuse flushes across 100 million split/delete/reuse transactions. The run found zero resurrected records and zero lost acknowledged commits, with worst-case recovery reads of 32 MiB per 100 GiB of index.” This identifies the tested setting without assigning an unstated crash count.
Should I call the result a completed design guarantee?

Report it as evidence from the completed extended run. It supports the stated recovery and reclamation behavior at its tested crash points, but it does not by itself specify every implementation rule or guarantee all possible executions. The concrete numbers and zero findings are the strongest precise way to state it.
Give me a concise final results sentence.
“Extended PhantomSplit-1: across 100 million transactions, there were zero resurrected records and zero lost acknowledged commits; worst-case recovery read 32 MiB per 100 GiB of index.”

For high churn, choose checkpointed quarantine-ring reclamation. The 100-million-transaction coverage at 32 MiB per 100 GiB outweighs the selector’s 28 MiB per 100 GiB over 10 million transactions. How should I state the decision?

“Choose checkpointed quarantine-ring reclamation for high-churn workloads: its 100-million-transaction coverage at 32 MiB of recovery reads per 100 GiB of index outweighs the selector’s lower 28 MiB per 100 GiB over 10 million transactions.” That makes both the choice and the reason explicit.
What does “outweighs” mean here?

It states the priority behind this decision. For high churn, you are placing greater weight on coverage at 100 million transactions than on the selector’s lower reported recovery-read figure over 10 million transactions. It does not mean 32 MiB is numerically less than 28 MiB.
Should I call the checkpointed approach faster?
No. The comparison is about recovery reads and transaction coverage, not elapsed time. It gives no basis for calling either approach faster.
The selector has the smaller read figure. Should the decision acknowledge that directly?

Yes. Saying “the selector’s 28 MiB per 100 GiB” makes the tradeoff clear: the checkpointed approach is being chosen for high churn despite the selector’s lower figure. Omitting that side of the comparison would obscure the stated reason for the choice.
How large is the difference in the two recovery-read figures?

They differ by 4 MiB per 100 GiB: 32 MiB per 100 GiB for the checkpointed approach versus 28 MiB per 100 GiB for the selector. That is an arithmetic comparison of the reported figures, not a claim that every recovery in the two runs read those exact amounts.
Can I describe the transaction coverage as tenfold?

The stated transaction counts are 100 million and 10 million, so the former is ten times the latter. If you use “tenfold,” attach it specifically to those transaction counts. Do not turn it into a claim of tenfold performance, tenfold crash coverage, or identical test conditions.
Does the choice mean 32 MiB per 100 GiB is a new recovery limit for the index?

No. Here, 32 MiB per 100 GiB is the figure associated with the 100-million-transaction coverage motivating this high-churn choice. The broader index goal retains its recovery-read requirement of at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB, independent of completed transaction count. The decision does not replace that requirement.
Should the 32 MiB figure be written without “per 100 GiB”?
Keep “per 100 GiB” on both figures. Otherwise the comparison would turn size-relative recovery-read figures into unqualified amounts and lose an important part of their meaning.
Am I choosing checkpointed quarantine-ring reclamation for every possible workload?
The decision specifies *high churn*. State the choice within that scope. It does not make a choice for every other workload or a general judgment about the selector outside this comparison.
What exactly am I choosing: a recovery procedure or a reclamation approach?

The named choice is checkpointed quarantine-ring *reclamation* for high churn. Its recovery-read figure and transaction coverage are the stated reasons for choosing it. Calling it solely a recovery procedure would leave out the reclamation decision.
Does the comparison establish that the two runs exercised identical conditions apart from transaction count?

No. The decision compares their stated transaction counts and recovery-read figures; it does not assert identical workloads, crash schedules, or measurement conditions. You can make the choice on the stated grounds without presenting the figures as a controlled, like-for-like performance comparison.
Can I say the selector cannot handle high churn?

That would go beyond this decision. Its stated reason is that the 100-million-transaction coverage at 32 MiB per 100 GiB outweighs the selector’s 28 MiB per 100 GiB over 10 million transactions for the high-churn choice. The comparison does not establish an inability to operate at a different transaction count.
Should I say the checkpointed approach has lower recovery reads under sustained churn?

No. The figures given are 32 MiB per 100 GiB and 28 MiB per 100 GiB; the checkpointed figure is higher. The advantage you are prioritizing is the stated 100-million-transaction coverage, not a lower read figure.
What if someone reads “coverage” as a guarantee for every future transaction count?

You can say “coverage across 100 million transactions” to anchor it to the stated scale. The choice does not by itself establish behavior at every greater transaction count or prove general independence from completed transaction count.
Does this decision also choose a concurrency-control method or root-publication protocol?

No such choice is made here. This decision names checkpointed quarantine-ring reclamation for high churn and gives a comparison of transaction coverage and recovery reads as its reason. It should not be expanded into decisions about other index components.
Give me a version that sounds decisive without overclaiming.

“For high-churn workloads, choose checkpointed quarantine-ring reclamation. Its coverage across 100 million transactions at 32 MiB of recovery reads per 100 GiB of index outweighs the selector’s lower 28 MiB per 100 GiB over 10 million transactions.”
The next plan is to implement the chosen quarantine-ring checkpoint rollover in the 16 MiB directory, then test billion-transaction churn for safe reuse and ≤32 MiB recovery. How should I state it?

State it as implementation and evaluation still to be done: implement quarantine-ring checkpoint rollover in the 16 MiB directory, then exercise a billion transactions of churn and check both safe reuse and whether recovery reads stay at or below 32 MiB. The plan gives a transaction scale and two evaluation targets; it reports no result from that test.
What is “rollover” referring to here?

It refers to moving the quarantine-ring checkpoint representation forward as churn continues, while keeping the information needed for safe reuse recoverable in the bounded directory. Here is a hypothesis about sustained reuse: per-extent epoch-stamped quarantine bitmaps checkpointed with shadow roots prevent resurrection through one billion reuses with ≤32 MiB of recovery reads. How should I frame it?

Frame it as a prediction, not an observed result: checkpoint per-extent epoch-stamped quarantine bitmaps together with shadow roots, and hypothesize that recovery can prevent reclaimed records from reappearing through one billion reuses while reading no more than 32 MiB. The design still has to show how a recovered root is matched to usable bitmap state, how the epoch stamps govern reuse, and what recovery must read to make safe decisions.
Does “one billion” refer to transactions?

No. In this hypothesis it refers specifically to one billion *reuses*. Do not substitute a transaction count, a crash count, or a number of reclaimed records. The hypothesis does not say how many transactions produce those reuses.

Not as stated. This hypothesis says ≤32 MiB of recovery reads without an index-size qualifier. Keep that separate from the broader recovery requirement, which is expressed per 100 GiB of index. Neither figure should silently acquire the other’s units.

It says the proposed quarantine bitmaps are associated with extents rather than described as one undifferentiated bitmap. That gives the hypothesis a scope for representing reuse state, but it does not specify an extent size, the number of extents, or how much bitmap data each extent requires.
Does it imply recovery must read a bitmap for every extent?

No. The hypothesis proposes a ≤32 MiB bound on total recovery reads; it does not specify which bitmaps recovery reads or when. If recovery needed every extent’s bitmap to establish a safe recovered state, those reads would have to fit the bound. Whether it can safely avoid some reads is a design question, not a consequence of the word “per-extent.”
What is an epoch stamp meant to distinguish?

Its intended role is to help interpret quarantine state across changes in a location’s lifetime. A stamp must have defined meaning relative to reuse and to the shadow root recovery selects; otherwise finding a stamp would not tell recovery whether an old reference can be treated as live. The hypothesis supplies no encoding, comparison rule, or epoch-advance procedure.
Can I say each reused slot receives a new epoch stamp?

That specific assignment rule is not stated. You can say the proposal uses epoch-stamped quarantine bitmaps to distinguish relevant reuse state. Whether stamps are attached to individual slots, bitmap states, or something else needs to be specified rather than inferred from the name.
Why are the bitmaps checkpointed with shadow roots?

A shadow root identifies an index view, while the bitmap information is meant to guide interpretation of quarantined and reusable locations. Checkpointing them together aims to give recovery a coherent root-and-reclamation state. The word “with” does not itself establish an atomic write or define how recovery identifies which checkpoint belongs to which root.
Could recovery select a root from one checkpoint and bitmap information from another?

It would need a sound reason to do so. The hypothesis depends on recovery interpreting the selected root using quarantine state appropriate to that root; an arbitrary mix could undermine the no-resurrection claim. A complete design must state which combinations are eligible after each relevant crash, rather than relying on the fact that both pieces are persistent.
Does a coherent root and bitmap automatically prevent resurrection?

No. Coherence is necessary to interpret them together, but the epoch stamps and quarantine rules must also correctly exclude reclaimed records. A consistently checkpointed state could still be unsafe if its rules permitted an old reference to count as live. Both publication and interpretation need an argument.
What if a crash interrupts checkpointing?

Recovery must not accept a partly published root-and-bitmap combination as a safe committed state merely because some pieces are readable. The hypothesis needs a way to identify a usable checkpoint or another valid recoverable state at that boundary. It does not prescribe a checkpoint format or an interrupted-publication rule.

The recovered state must not confuse the reused location’s current lifetime with a reclaimed record’s earlier lifetime. The selected root and epoch-stamped quarantine information must support that distinction even across the crash. The hypothesis predicts no resurrection through one billion reuses, but does not yet demonstrate it for this or any other crash case.
Does “prevent resurrection” mean reuse must be prohibited?

No. The hypothesis explicitly speaks of one billion reuses. Its predicted property is that performing those reuses does not cause a reclaimed record to reappear as live after recovery. Permitted use of a location for a later record is different from resurrection of its former record.
Do the bitmaps have to retain the entire history of those reuses?

The hypothesis does not say they retain each reuse as a separate event. No. This is a hypothesis about non-resurrection through one billion reuses and ≤32 MiB recovery reads. Where should slot reuse fall in the reasoning?

What must be true immediately before a reuse is allowed?

Does the ordering have to account for a crash after the bitmap checkpoint but before the root checkpoint?

What about a crash after the root checkpoint but before reuse?

The safety condition concerns what the recovered state actually says about the slot, not just the fact that the root checkpoint exists.

The recoverable state must distinguish the prior reclaimed record from any new lifetime of the location. The exact crash states depend on an implementation that has not been specified here.

Not automatically. If a slot was reused or a root was made recoverable under later state, an older checkpoint might not describe the lifetime correctly. A fallback must be justified for the same recovered state, rather than treated as safe merely because it is older.
Is the problem specifically that the bitmap checkpoint might be partially written?
