I propose combining fence-version validation with bitmap-before-root checkpoints, post-checkpoint reuse, and dual 24 MiB extent directories. How should I present this persistent-memory transactional index design?

Present it as one proposal with linked concurrency and recovery obligations. Fence-version validation is intended to protect the predicates on which transactions depend. Bitmap-before-root checkpoints and post-checkpoint reuse are intended to keep the root and reclamation state consistently interpretable across crashes. Dual 24 MiB extent directories are the proposed bounded structures for extent state. The proposal still needs to show that acknowledged commits survive every injected persistence-boundary crash, reclaimed records do not reappear, and recovery reads at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index independently of completed transaction count.
What does fence-version validation contribute that the other components do not?

It addresses whether concurrent transactions can be accepted with serializable outcomes. In particular, a scan can depend on an entire range, including the absence of qualifying records. Fence-version validation is meant to make relevant changes to that range detectable. Checkpoints, reuse rules, and extent directories address different questions about persistent state and record lifetimes; they do not themselves validate a range predicate.
Does naming fence-version validation establish that a range scan cannot miss a phantom?

No. The design must define what each recorded fence version covers and why a change that matters to a scan will be detected before its transaction is accepted. That includes changes represented across leaf splits. This proposal names the validation approach, but does not supply its complete rules or a new finding about serializability.
Why is the bitmap-before-root order part of the same proposal?

A recovered root must be interpreted using reclamation information that is safe for that root. Persisting the relevant bitmap checkpoint before the root checkpoint is intended to keep recovery from selecting a root whose required bitmap state is unavailable. The order needs a publication and selection rule as well: merely finding persistent bitmap data does not establish which root it belongs with.
Does bitmap-before-root mean both checkpoints become durable in one atomic operation?

No. It describes an ordering between persistence steps, not a single atomic write. The design must say which checkpoint combinations recovery may select if a crash interrupts either step, and why each selectable combination preserves acknowledged commits without resurrecting reclaimed records.
Where does post-checkpoint reuse fit in that sequence?

It places reuse after the checkpoint relevant to interpreting the slot’s prior lifetime. That is meant to prevent reuse from getting ahead of recoverable quarantine state. The proposal does not define how many reuses a checkpoint covers, when an individual slot becomes eligible, or the exact operations involved in reuse.
Is a reused slot itself a resurrected record?

No. A slot may enter a new lifetime through permitted reuse. Resurrection means that recovery treats its earlier reclaimed record as live again. The proposed checkpoint ordering and reuse constraint have to preserve that distinction after a crash.
What are the extent directories supposed to do?

They are proposed as bounded places to represent extent-related state that recovery may need. Their role must be specified in relation to the selected root, bitmap checkpoints, and reuse decisions. Having directories does not by itself establish that they contain sufficient information or that recovery can choose a coherent directory state after an interrupted update.
How should I read “dual 24 MiB extent directories”?

It specifies two extent directories of 24 MiB each. Together their stated capacities total 48 MiB. That is arithmetic about the directories, not a measured recovery-read count: the proposal does not say whether recovery reads both in full, reads only portions, or needs other data as well.
If the two directories total 48 MiB, can I immediately say the 64 MiB per 100 GiB recovery cap is met?

No. You would need to count every read required to establish a safe recovered state, including any root, checkpoint, or selection information beyond the directories. Also, the cap is expressed per 100 GiB of index, while the two stated directory sizes are fixed component sizes. Their numerical comparison alone does not prove the size-relative limit for all index sizes.
Could I claim recovery always reads exactly 48 MiB?
Not from the proposal. Forty-eight MiB is the sum of two 24 MiB directory sizes, not a prescribed or observed recovery path. An exact read count would require knowing what recovery actually accesses.
Why have two directories rather than one?

The dual arrangement suggests maintaining candidate extent-directory states so an update need not erase every alternative state recovery could inspect. But this proposal does not specify how the two are updated, which is selectable, or how recovery handles an interrupted change. The reason to name both in the design is to make those selection and consistency questions explicit, not to assume they are answered by duplication.
Can recovery simply select whichever directory looks newer?

Apparent recency alone is not a crash-safety rule. Recovery needs a justified way to select a complete directory state that agrees with its selected root and bitmap checkpoint. If it combines independently chosen pieces, it might interpret a reused slot under the wrong lifetime state.
What is the central invariant tying these parts together?

Every state recovery may select must provide a committed root together with extent and bitmap information sufficient to interpret its record lifetimes safely. It must contain every commit already acknowledged before the crash and must not make a reclaimed record live again. Fence-version validation has a related but distinct obligation: transactions accepted into such a state must have serializable outcomes.
Could fence-version validation pass while this recovery invariant fails?

Yes. Transactions could have serializable outcomes during execution, while an interrupted checkpoint or mismatched directory causes recovery to lose an acknowledged commit or resurrect a reclaimed record. Conversely, recovery could faithfully preserve a committed state whose transactions were not serializable. The proposal combines mechanisms because both sides must hold.
How does an acknowledgment enter the proposed checkpoint scheme?

The design needs to define when a commit may be acknowledged relative to a root state that recovery can select. After acknowledgment, no injected persistence-boundary crash may cause recovery to omit that commit. This proposal does not specify that point; bitmap-before-root ordering alone does not define an acknowledgment rule.
What would a crash between the bitmap checkpoint and the root checkpoint require?

Recovery would need to select a valid committed root and compatible reclamation state without interpreting an uncompleted root checkpoint as committed. It also must preserve any commits already acknowledged. Whether a newly persistent bitmap checkpoint can be used with that selected root depends on rules the proposal has not supplied.
And a crash after the root checkpoint but before reuse?

Recovery must be able to interpret the selected root with its associated bitmap and directory state. It should not infer that a slot has entered a new lifetime merely because the checkpoints exist; reuse is a separate event under the proposed post-checkpoint rule. The precise recovered interpretation depends on the publication and reuse rules still to be defined.
What if a crash occurs during reuse?

The recoverable state must continue to distinguish the reclaimed record’s earlier lifetime from any later one. Recovery cannot make the old record live or drop an acknowledged commit because it selected mismatched root, bitmap, or directory information. The proposal identifies the ordering constraint, but not the persistent states possible during an individual reuse.
Does this design require scanning completed transactions to reconstruct extent state?

It must not rely on reads that grow with completed transaction count if it is to meet the index goal. The directories and checkpoints are proposed places for bounded current evidence, but their presence alone does not show that recovery can avoid consulting accumulated history. The design must explain why current published state remains sufficient as transactions complete.
Is the recovery limit a cap on fence-version validation reads as well?

No. The numerical limit—at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB of index, independent of completed transaction count—concerns recovery reads. First, do fence versions cover all relevant scan predicates so accepted transactions are serializable? Second, which root, bitmap checkpoint, and extent-directory state may recovery select at each injected persistence-boundary crash? Third, when may a slot be reused without making its prior reclaimed record live after recovery? Fourth, when is a commit safe to acknowledge? No. This node is a proposal to combine fence-version validation, bitmap-before-root checkpoints, post-checkpoint reuse, and dual 24 MiB extent directories. It does not state an implementation decision, a completed test, or a judgment about any other design.

The broader index requirement rules out recovery reads that grow with completed transaction count. The question itself does not prescribe a replay mechanism.

For each relevant persistence boundary during rollover, determine what is durably visible in both directories, what bitmap checkpoint is actually complete, which root is recoverably committed, and which combinations recovery may select. What crash-safe completion, ordering, and root-association rule lets the dual 24 MiB extent directories identify the latest eligible complete bitmap checkpoint when rollover is interrupted, without losing acknowledged commits, reviving reclaimed records, or requiring recovery reads that grow with completed transactions?

My hypothesis is that CRC-protected generation headers and an atomic root epoch can select the newest complete directory after a crash, discarding interrupted rollover checkpoints. How should I frame it?

Frame it as a proposed recovery-selection rule, not an established result. Should I say the CRC proves the entire directory was written successfully?

No. The hypothesis specifies CRC-protected generation headers, not necessarily a CRC covering every byte of a directory or its bitmap checkpoint. The design has to define what the CRC covers and what a passing check establishes. It cannot infer completeness of unprotected data merely from a valid header.
Could the highest generation number simply be the newest complete directory?

Not without the completeness check. An interrupted rollover might leave a candidate with a higher generation header while other information needed for that candidate is incomplete. Recovery would need to consider only eligible complete candidates, then use a defined ordering to identify the newest among them.
Where does the atomic root epoch enter that ordering?

The hypothesis uses it to tie directory selection to a recoverable root state. It should prevent recovery from treating a directory generation as eligible merely because it appears newer, if that generation is not appropriate for the selected root epoch. Exactly how epochs and generations correspond is not stated; that relationship is part of what the hypothesis must define.
Does calling the root epoch atomic mean all root and directory updates are atomic together?

No. “Atomic root epoch” is the proposed atomic element, not a claim that an entire root, a directory, and a bitmap checkpoint change in one indivisible operation. The hypothesis still needs to show what recovery can observe when a crash interrupts the surrounding rollover and how it selects a coherent combination.
Can the CRC and root epoch together tell us which checkpoint to discard?

That is the prediction. Recovery would need a rule that rejects an interrupted rollover checkpoint rather than mistaking it for the newest complete one. The CRC-protected headers and atomic root epoch are the proposed evidence for that rule; the hypothesis does not yet demonstrate that they distinguish every complete candidate from every interrupted one.
Does “discarding” mean erasing the interrupted checkpoint during recovery?

Not necessarily. In this hypothesis, the essential meaning is that recovery does not select or rely on an interrupted rollover checkpoint as its committed state. Whether any stored data is physically erased is not specified.
What if both directories have headers whose CRC checks pass?

Passing header checks would leave recovery to determine whether each candidate is complete and eligible for the atomic root epoch it observes. If both qualify, it needs a sound generation-order rule to select the newest complete directory. The hypothesis does not specify the exact comparison or imply that CRC validity alone chooses between them.
What if the newer-looking header passes its CRC but the associated bitmap checkpoint is incomplete?

Then a sound completeness rule would have to reject that candidate despite the passing header CRC. This is why the proposed header protection cannot stand in for an argument about everything a complete checkpoint requires. The hypothesis aims to discard interrupted rollover checkpoints, so this case must be addressed rather than assumed impossible.
Could recovery choose the other directory in that situation?

Only if the other directory is complete and compatible with the recoverable root epoch, and selecting it does not lose an acknowledged commit or misinterpret reclaimed records. Having a second candidate makes fallback possible in principle; it does not make fallback automatically safe.
What if the other directory is complete but older than the root epoch?

The hypothesis needs to define whether that directory is eligible for that root at all. Completeness in isolation does not establish that its bitmap state correctly interprets the selected root. Recovery cannot treat an older candidate as safe merely because its header passes a CRC.
And if neither directory qualifies?

The hypothesis would need to explain how recovery establishes a valid committed state in that crash case. It must not quietly choose an interrupted checkpoint just to have a candidate. The statement that the headers and root epoch select the newest complete directory depends on showing what valid candidate remains at each relevant interrupted-rollover boundary.
Is it fair to treat the root epoch as a publication indicator?

That is a way to express its intended role, provided the design defines precisely what an atomic root-epoch value certifies. The hypothesis does not specify how the value is made durable or exactly when a root becomes eligible. Publication, acknowledgment, and directory completeness still need a consistent relationship across crashes.
Why does acknowledgment matter when the immediate question is directory selection?

Because selecting an older complete directory and root could be incorrect if it drops a commit that was already acknowledged. The recovery rule must discard interrupted rollover checkpoints without discarding acknowledged commits. The hypothesis names the root epoch as part of selection but does not yet define the acknowledgment boundary.
What is the reclamation-safety side of choosing the newest complete directory?

The chosen directory must carry bitmap checkpoint information appropriate to the selected root, so recovery does not treat a reclaimed record as live or confuse an earlier slot lifetime with a later one. Selecting a numerically newer generation is useful only if its information is complete and safe for that root. This remains a required property to establish, not an observed result of the hypothesis.
Could a complete directory still be unsafe?

Yes. “Complete” might mean all its required contents are durable, while “safe to select” also requires that those contents correspond to the committed root and correctly interpret reclamation state. The proposed rule needs both conditions. A passing CRC, a complete candidate, and a matching root cannot be treated as interchangeable claims.
Does this hypothesis specify a recovery-read bound?

No numerical recovery-read bound is stated in this hypothesis. It addresses how to identify the newest complete directory and discard interrupted rollover checkpoints. The overall index still requires recovery reads of at most 64 MiB per 100 GiB, independent of completed transaction count, so the eventual selection rule must work within that separate constraint.
Do we need to read every historical rollover checkpoint to find the newest one?

An answer to the bounded-recovery question should not depend on searching an accumulation of completed rollover history. The hypothesis proposes using generation headers in the dual directories and the atomic root epoch as current selection evidence. It still must show that this evidence is sufficient after interruptions and that required recovery reads do not grow with completed transaction count.
Can I say reading the two directory headers alone always suffices?

Not from the hypothesis as stated. Recovery might need additional reads to determine whether a bitmap checkpoint is complete and compatible with the selected root. Header reads alone are sufficient only if the eventual protocol establishes that they certify every condition recovery needs. No such read-path guarantee is given here.
How should I analyze a crash during rollover without inventing a particular flush sequence?

For each persistence boundary the eventual protocol exposes, ask which generation headers can be trusted under their CRC checks, which directory and bitmap checkpoint candidates are complete, and what root epoch recovery can select. Then test whether the selection rule rejects interrupted checkpoints while preserving acknowledged commits and reclaimed-record safety. This describes the necessary cases without asserting an update sequence the hypothesis has not supplied.

A crash state in which recovery accepts an interrupted rollover checkpoint as the newest complete directory would contradict it. These are possible checks, not reported outcomes.

The completeness, generation-order, and root-matching rules—and their behavior at each relevant crash boundary—remain to be established.

It checks that a slot’s earlier reclaimed record does not appear live after recovery. A location safely reused for a later record is different from the reclaimed record reappearing. The result must be judged against that record-lifetime distinction, not merely against whether a reused slot exists.
